Highest score achieved, by year

Geography/Geology (Paper Code 313) highest NTA score, by year: 2022 — 200/200 (full marks, named toppers, sourced from NTA's own subject-wise result releases); 2023 — 183/200; 2024 — 200/200, achieved by 373 candidates (NTA release); 2025 — 250/250, full marks (NTA release — the marks ceiling itself rose to 250 that year); 2026 — 249.45/250 (NTA release).

A short prep checklist

Read the NCERT textbook fully at least once before jumping straight into practice questions — CUET stays close to NCERT's own wording.

Learn the maps and figures alongside the text — Geography MCQs frequently reference locations, regions and distribution patterns shown in NCERT's own figures and tables.

Solve real practice questions by topic first — untimed, to build accuracy — then move to timed practice to build speed.

Take at least one full 60-minute mock at real exam pace before exam day, not just topic-wise practice.

Revisit your wrong answers weekly — a mistake reviewed once is often repeated; review it until it stops happening.

Prioritise High-importance topics first — check the Chapters tab for our topic-importance ranking, and start with what's flagged High before Medium or Low.

Know your skip threshold — decide in advance how confident you need to be before attempting an unsure question, given the −1 negative marking.

Spend the final week revising, not learning new topics — consolidate facts and definitions using each chapter's Cheat Sheet rather than starting fresh material.

Chapter importance is our own editorial judgement, based on the weightage patterns we generally see in CUET Geography papers — not an official NTA ranking.

    Formula Vault — every formula in the chapter

    No exceptions, no explanations — every formula from this chapter, serially numbered, ready for a final scan.

    Group A — Growth & Density (3 formulas)
    1

    Decadal Growth Rate

    g = [(P₂ − P₁) ÷ P₁] × 100
    2

    Physiological Density

    Physiological Density = Total Population ÷ Net Cultivated Area
    3

    Agricultural Density

    Agricultural Density = Total Agricultural Population ÷ Net Cultivable Area

    Key Facts, Topic by Topic

    Every load-bearing number, grouped by topic, in one scannable grid.

    Sources & Distribution

    • First Census: 1872; first complete: 1881; every 10 years.
    • Highest population: UP > Maharashtra > Bihar > West Bengal. Top 10 states = ~76%.
    • Smallest shares: J&K (1.04%), Arunachal Pradesh (0.11%), Uttarakhand (0.84%).

    Density

    • India 2011: 382/km² (1951: 117/km²).
    • Highest: Delhi (11,297/km²). Lowest: Arunachal Pradesh (17/km²).
    • Physiological = Pop ÷ Net Cultivated Area. Agricultural = Agri. Pop ÷ Net Cultivable Area.

    Growth

    • Annual (2011): 1.64%. Decadal (2001–11): 17.64%. Only negative decade: 1911–21 (−0.31%).
    • 4 Phases: I Stagnant (1901–21) · II Steady (1921–51) · III Explosion (1951–81, avg 2.2%/yr) · IV Slowdown (1981–present).
    • Projected 2025 population: 1,350 million.

    Regional Variation

    • Lowest growth (1991–2001): Kerala 9.4%.
    • 2001–11: Maharashtra fell most (−6.7 pts); Tamil Nadu & Puducherry rose.

    Adolescents

    • 20.9% aged 10–19 (52.7% M / 47.3% F).
    • NYP–2014: 'youth' = 15–29 years. Skill Policy: 2015.

    Rural–Urban

    • 68.8% rural, 31.16% urban. 6,40,867 villages, 93.2% inhabited.
    • Very rural: HP, Bihar. ~Half rural: Goa, Mizoram.

    Language

    • Grierson: 179 languages, 544 dialects. Today: ~22 scheduled.
    • Indo-European 73% · Dravidian 20% · Austric 1.38% · Sino-Tibetan 0.85%.

    Religion (2011)

    • Hindus 79.8% · Muslims 14.2% · Christians 2.3% · Sikhs 1.7% · Buddhists 0.7% · Jains 0.4%.
    • Muslim majority: Kashmir valley, Lakshadweep.

    Working Population

    • Main ≥183 days/yr; Marginal <183 days/yr. Workers 39.8%.
    • Primary 54.6% · Secondary 3.8% · Tertiary 41.6%. Primary fell from 58.2% (2001).

    The Four Growth Phases, compact

    Phase I1901–1921 · Stagnant
    Health & sanitation improve
    Phase II1921–1951 · Steady
    Mortality crashes, births stay high
    Phase III1951–1981 · Explosion
    Birth rate finally falls
    Phase IV1981–present · Slowdown

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Distribution

    Physical factors decide the base pattern; socio-economic factors (irrigation, minerals, transport, industry) redraw it.

    Density types

    Plain density = people ÷ ALL land. Physiological density = people ÷ FARMED land — always the bigger, truer number.

    Growth phases

    Stagnant → Steady → Explosion → Slowdown. Deaths fall first (Phase II–III); births fall last (Phase IV).

    Language shares

    Indo-European ≈ ¾ of India (73%). Dravidian ≈ ⅕ (20%). Austric + Sino-Tibetan together barely cross 2%.

    Muslim majority regions

    Only TWO places: the Kashmir valley and Lakshadweep. Everywhere else, "largest minority" ≠ "majority."

    Main vs Marginal worker

    183 days = 6 months. At or above it → MAIN. Below it → MARGINAL.

    Rural vs Urban

    Rural is bigger in share (68.8%) but urban is bigger in growth RATE — don't confuse the two.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 15 definitions

    1. Density of population: "expressed as number of persons per unit area."

    2. Physiological density: "total population ÷ net cultivated area."

    3. Agricultural density: "total agricultural population ÷ net cultivable area."

    4. Agricultural population: "includes cultivators and agricultural labourers and their family members."

    5. Growth of population: "the change in the number of people living in a particular area between two points of time... expressed in percentage."

    6. Natural growth: assessed "by assessing the crude birth and death rates."

    7. Induced growth: "explained by the volume of inward and outward movement of people."

    8. Population doubling time: "the time taken by any population to double itself at its current annual growth rate."

    9. Decadal growth rate: g = [(P₂ − P₁) ÷ P₁] × 100.

    10. Main worker: "a person who works for atleast 183 days (or six months) in a year."

    11. Marginal worker: "a person who works for less than 183 days (or six months) in a year."

    12. National Youth Policy 'youth': "persons in the age group of 15–29 years."

    13. Population composition: "a distinct field of study within population geography with a vast coverage of analysis of age and sex, place of residence, ethnic characteristics, tribes, language, religion, marital status, literacy and education, occupational characteristics, etc."

    14. Occupational categories (2011 Census): "cultivators, agricultural labourers, household industrial workers, and other workers."

    15. Work participation rate: proportion of the working population to total population.

    Non-negotiables to remember

    • Delhi has the highest density, not the highest population — Uttar Pradesh has the highest population.
    • Physiological density is always larger than crude density, since it divides by a smaller denominator (cultivated land only).
    • Phase III's "explosion" is caused by falling death rate + still-high birth rate — not two high rates together.
    • Muslims form a majority only in the Kashmir valley and Lakshadweep — everywhere else, "largest minority" (14.2%) does not mean majority.
    • Linguistic regions in India do not have sharp boundaries — they merge and overlap.
    • Work participation rate tends to be higher where economic development is lower.
    • The agricultural sector's worker share is declining (58.2% in 2001 → 54.6% in 2011) as workers shift to non-farm sectors.
    • A blind guess still carries positive expected value under CUET's marking scheme — never leave an MCQ blank.

    1. Distribution is uneven: UP, Maharashtra, Bihar, WB lead; J&K, Arunachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand trail despite large area.
    2. Density = 382/km² (2011), up from 117/km² (1951). Delhi highest (11,297), Arunachal Pradesh lowest (17).
    3. Physiological density = Population ÷ Net Cultivated Area — always bigger than crude density.
    4. Four growth phases: Stagnant (1901–21) → Steady (1921–51) → Explosion (1951–81) → Slowdown (1981–present).
    5. Kerala's 9.4% was the lowest decadal growth rate (1991–2001); Maharashtra fell the most (−6.7 pts) in the next decade.
    6. Rural 68.8%, Urban 31.16% (2011) — 6,40,867 villages, 93.2% inhabited.
    7. Language: Indo-European 73%, Dravidian 20%, Austric 1.38%, Sino-Tibetan 0.85%.
    8. Religion: Hindus 79.8%, Muslims 14.2% (majority only in Kashmir valley & Lakshadweep).
    9. Main worker ≥183 days/yr; Marginal worker <183 days/yr. Workers = 39.8% of population.
    10. Sectors: Primary 54.6%, Secondary 3.8%, Tertiary 41.6% — primary share falling, a sectoral shift underway.
    Notes prepared from NCERT "India: People and Economy," Class XII, Chapter 1 — Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition, for CUET revision.

    Cheat Sheet & Mnemonics

    Everything on one scroll — classifications, definitions, and the glossary. Read this the night before the exam.

    Key Facts, Topic by Topic

    Every load-bearing fact, grouped by topic, in one scannable grid.

    Meaning & Types

    • Rural = land-based primary activities. Urban = manufacturing + services.
    • Cities are nodes of economic growth, linked to rural hinterlands via transport & communication.

    Rural Settlement Types

    • 4 types: Clustered, Semi-Clustered, Hamleted, Dispersed.
    • Driven by physical, cultural/ethnic, and security factors.

    Urban — Census Definition

    • Min. population 5,000 · ≥75% male workers non-agri · density ≥400/km².
    • Plus municipality, corporation, cantonment board, or notified town area committee.

    Evolution of Towns

    • Ancient (2,000+ yrs) · Medieval (~100 towns) · Modern (British, post-1850 industrial).
    • 3 British nodes: Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata.

    Urbanisation

    • 2011 level: 31.16%. 20th-century growth: 11-fold.
    • Decennial growth rate peaked 1971–81 (46.14%), has cooled since.

    Functional Classification

    • 9 classes: Admin, Industrial, Transport, Commercial, Mining, Garrison, Educational, Religious/Cultural, Tourist.
    • Cities become multifunctional as they grow into metropolises.

    Evolution of Towns, compact

    Ancient2,000+ yrs · religious/cultural
    Fort towns rise on their ruins
    Medieval~100 towns · kingdom HQs
    Europeans arrive, 18th century
    ModernPorts → 3 nodes → post-1850 industry

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Rural vs Urban

    Rural = land feeds you; Urban = factories and services employ you. Connected by transport & communication.

    Four rural settlement types

    Clustered = compact & together. Semi-clustered = together, but class-divided. Hamleted = split into named pieces. Dispersed = scattered, isolated huts.

    Census urban formula

    5 / 75 / 400 — population ≥5,000, ≥75% male workers non-agri, density ≥400/km².

    Three eras of towns

    Ancient = religion (Varanasi, Madurai). Medieval = forts & kingdoms (Delhi, Jaipur, Agra). Modern = the British — Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata.

    Multifunctional cities

    Cities are dynamic, not static — as they grow into metropolises, several functions get intertwined.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every formal definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 6 definitions

    1. Human Settlement: "cluster of dwellings of any type or size where human beings live."

    2. Urban settlement (Census 1991): "All places which have municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee and have a minimum population of 5000 persons, at least 75 per cent of male workers are engaged in non-agriculture pursuits and a density of population of at least 400 persons per square kilometer."

    3. Clustered settlement: "a compact or closely built up area of houses" — the general living area distinct from surrounding farms, barns and pastures.

    4. Level of urbanisation: "measured in terms of percentage of urban population to total population."

    5. Functional classification of towns: classification "on the basis of dominant or specialised functions."

    6. Smart Cities Mission: objective "to promote cities that provide core infrastructure, a clean and sustainable environment and give a decent quality of life to its citizens."

    Must Remember Numbers

    Every number worth having ready in your head before you open the paper.

    Functional classes of Indian towns, per NCERT

    Non-negotiables to remember

    • The Census urban definition needs ALL FOUR conditions together — administrative status, population, worker composition, AND density — not just one.
    • 75% of male workers in NON-agriculture, not agriculture — a classic reversed-option trap.
    • Medieval fort towns were built on the ruins of ancient towns, not on empty ground.
    • Semi-Clustered settlements come from splitting an existing village, not from new people moving into empty land.
    • India's urban share keeps rising, but its decennial growth rate has been falling since 1971–81 — two different numbers.
    • Varanasi is classed under both Educational AND Religious/Cultural towns — dominant function isn't the only function.
    • A blind guess still carries positive expected value under CUET's marking scheme — never leave an MCQ blank.

    One Minute Revision

    Read this, then close the laptop

    1. Rural vs Urban: primary activities vs manufacturing/services; cities are nodes of growth; rural relations intimate, urban formal.
    2. 4 rural settlement types: Clustered (compact), Semi-Clustered (split by class), Hamleted (split into named units), Dispersed (isolated huts).
    3. Census urban formula: 5,000+ population, ≥75% male workers non-agri, ≥400/km² density, plus municipal-type status.
    4. Ancient towns: 2,000+ yrs, religious/cultural — Varanasi, Prayagraj, Patna, Madurai.
    5. Medieval towns: ~100 towns, fort/kingdom HQs — Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Agra.
    6. Modern towns: British — 3 nodes (Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata); post-1850 industrial e.g. Jamshedpur.
    7. Urbanisation, 2011: 31.16% of India is urban — 11-fold rise across the 20th century, but growth rate has slowed since 1971–81.
    8. 9 functional classes: Admin, Industrial, Transport, Commercial, Mining, Garrison, Educational, Religious/Cultural, Tourist.
    9. Smart Cities Mission: core infrastructure + sustainability + quality of life, via compact, replicable models.
    10. Cities are dynamic — as they grow into metropolises, they become multifunctional.

    Formula Vault

    The chapter's one formula, serially numbered, ready for a final scan.

    Group A — Land Use (1 formula)
    1

    Cropping Intensity

    CI (%) = (Gross Cropped Area ÷ Net Sown Area) × 100

    Key Facts, Topic by Topic

    Every load-bearing number, grouped by topic, in one scannable grid.

    Land Use Categories

    • 9 categories; add up to reporting area (≠ fixed geographical area).
    • 1950-51→2019-20: 5 up (forest, non-agri use, pasture, current fallow, net sown), 4 down (barren/waste, culturable waste, tree crops, fallow-other).

    CPR & Cultivable Land

    • Total cultivable land: 59.5% → 57.7% of reporting area (1950-51→2019-20).
    • Formula: Net Sown + all Fallow + Culturable Wasteland.

    Cropping Seasons

    • Kharif (Jun–Sep, monsoon) · Rabi (Oct–Mar, winter) · Zaid (Apr–Jun, short summer).
    • CI = GCA ÷ NSA × 100. Dryland farming: <75cm rainfall.

    Cereals

    • ~54% of cropped area; India 3rd in world (~11%).
    • Rice ~25% (2nd in world) · Wheat ~14% (UP leads) · coarse cereals ~16.5% combined.

    Pulses & Oilseeds

    • Pulses ~11% (Gram, Tur) · Oilseeds ~14% (Groundnut, Rapeseed/Mustard, Soyabean).
    • Groundnut = 18.8% of world output (2018).

    Fibre & Plantation Crops

    • Cotton — 2nd in world; ~4.7% cropped area. Jute — WB ~75% of output.
    • Sugarcane — UP ~40%. Tea — Assam 53.2%. Coffee — Karnataka >67%.

    Agricultural Development

    • Green Revolution: HYV wheat (Mexico) + rice (Philippines), mid-1960s.
    • Started in Punjab/Haryana/W.UP/AP/Gujarat. Fertiliser use up 15× since mid-1960s.

    Problems of Agriculture

    • Only ~33% irrigated. Zamindari = most exploitative revenue system.
    • Seasonal unemployment: 4–8 months in unirrigated tracts.

    Agricultural Development, compact

    Pre-1947Subsistence, droughts, famines
    IADP, IAAP launched
    Mid-1960sHYV seeds — Green Revolution begins
    Spreads nationwide post-1970s
    1988 onwardAgro-climatic planning, liberalisation (1990s)

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Land-use trend

    5 up, 4 down since 1950-51: Forests, Non-agri use, Pasture, Current fallow, Net sown ROSE. Barren/waste, Culturable waste, Tree crops, Fallow-other FELL.

    CPR

    Community-owned, no one's private property — vital for the landless. Total cultivable land = Net Sown + all Fallow + Culturable Wasteland.

    Three seasons

    Kharif = monsoon-sown. Rabi = winter-sown. Zaid = short summer gap-filler.

    State ↔ crop

    Assam = tea. West Bengal = jute. Uttar Pradesh = sugarcane. Karnataka = coffee.

    Green Revolution

    HYV seed + irrigation + fertiliser, born in Punjab/Haryana/W.UP, mid-1960s.

    Irrigation gap

    Only ⅓ of cultivated land is irrigated — the rest gambles on the monsoon.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every formal definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 6 definitions

    1. Culturable Wasteland: land left fallow (uncultivated) for more than five years.

    2. Current Fallow: land left without cultivation for one or less than one agricultural year.

    3. Net Area Sown: "the physical extent of land on which crops are sown and harvested."

    4. Common Property Resources (CPRs): "community's natural resource, where every member has the right of access and usage with specified obligations, without anybody having property rights over them."

    5. Cropping Intensity: (Gross Cropped Area ÷ Net Sown Area) × 100.

    6. Pulses: "legume crops which increase the natural fertility of soils through nitrogen fixation."

    Must Remember Numbers

    Every number worth having ready in your head before you open the paper.

    59.5% → 57.7%
    Total cultivable land, 1950-51 → 2019-20
    ~54%
    Cereals' share of total cropped area
    ~25% / ~14%
    Rice / Wheat share of cropped area
    2nd
    India's world rank in cotton & sugarcane production
    53.2%

    Mexico / Philippines
    Origin of HYV wheat / rice seeds
    1988
    Year agro-climatic planning was initiated
    15×
    Rise in fertiliser use since the mid-1960s
    ~33%

    4–8 months
    Seasonal unemployment in unirrigated tracts

    Non-negotiables to remember

    • Reporting area ≠ geographical area — reporting area can shift with land revenue estimates; geographical area (Survey of India) stays fixed.
    • Culturable wasteland (>5 yrs) vs fallow other than current (1–5 yrs) vs current fallow (≤1 yr) — differ only by duration.
    • Protective irrigation spreads limited water over maximum area; productive irrigation concentrates more water for higher yield — opposite goals.
    • Maize is grown all over India except Punjab and the eastern/north-eastern regions — a common reversed-option trap.
    • Rice cultivation in Punjab and Haryana is not traditional — it was introduced in the 1970s, post-Green Revolution.
    • Only ⅓ of cultivated area is irrigated in India — the rest depends directly on the monsoon.
    • A blind guess still carries positive expected value under CUET's marking scheme — never leave an MCQ blank.

    Read this, then close the laptop

    1. 9 land-use categories add up to reporting area; 5 rose, 4 fell since 1950-51.
    2. Total cultivable land: 59.5% → 57.7% of reporting area (1950-51→2019-20).
    3. 3 cropping seasons: Kharif (monsoon), Rabi (winter), Zaid (short summer).
    4. Cereals = ~54% of cropped area; rice ~25%, wheat ~14%.
    5. Pulses ~11% (Gram, Tur); Oilseeds ~14% (Groundnut, Rapeseed/Mustard, Soyabean).
    6. Cotton 2nd in world; Sugarcane 2nd in world; Jute — WB ~75%; Tea — Assam 53.2%; Coffee — Karnataka >67%.
    7. Green Revolution: HYV wheat (Mexico) + rice (Philippines), mid-1960s, started in Punjab/Haryana/W.UP.
    8. Agro-climatic planning from 1988; liberalisation from the 1990s.
    9. Only ⅓ of cultivated area is irrigated — the rest depends on the monsoon.
    10. Land degradation: salinisation/waterlogging in irrigated areas; erosion in rainfed areas.

    Key Facts, Topic by Topic

    Every load-bearing number, grouped by topic, in one scannable grid.

    Water Resources of India

    • 4% of world's water, >17% of world's population, 2.45% of world area.
    • 4,000 km³ precipitation → 1,869 km³ available → 1,122 km³ utilisable.

    Water Demand & Utilisation

    • Agriculture: 89% surface water, 92% groundwater.
    • Punjab wells/tubewells 76.1%, Haryana 51.3% of net irrigated area.

    Emerging Water Problems

    • Yamuna = most polluted river (Delhi–Etawah). CPCB: 507 stations.
    • Water Act 1974, Environment Protection Act 1986 — under-enforced.

    Water Conservation & Management

    • Kund/Tanka (Rajasthan). Atal Bhujal Yojana: 7 states, 80 districts.
    • Ralegan Siddhi case study. Jal Kranti Abhiyan: 1 Jal Gram/district, 672 districts.

    Water availability, compact

    4,000 km³Total precipitation, annually
    Surface + groundwater
    1,869 km³Available (surface + replenishable GW)
    Only 60% usable
    1,122 km³Total utilisable water resource

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Water squeeze

    4,000 → 1,869 → 1,122 (cubic km): total precipitation → available → utilisable. Only 60% of what's available can be used.

    Sector shares

    Agriculture: 89% surface, 92% groundwater. Domestic share is HIGHER in surface water (9%) than groundwater (3%) — the reverse of the usual assumption.

    Most polluted

    Yamuna, between Delhi and Etawah. CPCB monitors 507 stations; organic/bacterial contamination is the main pollutant.

    Conservation

    Kund/Tanka = Rajasthan. Atal Bhujal Yojana = 7 states, 80 districts, 8,220 panchayats. Ralegan Siddhi = Maharashtra case study.

    Two under-enforced Acts

    Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and Environment Protection Act, 1986 — both cited as poorly implemented.

    Fluoride vs Arsenic

    Fluoride rises in Rajasthan & Maharashtra; Arsenic rises in West Bengal & Bihar — both from over-withdrawal of groundwater.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every formal definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 5 definitions

    1. Water Quality: "purity of water, or water without unwanted foreign substances."

    2. Watershed Management: "efficient management and conservation of surface and groundwater resources" through prevention of runoff, storage and recharge.

    3. Rainwater Harvesting: "a method to capture and store rainwater for various uses," also used to recharge groundwater aquifers.

    4. Kund / Tanka: a covered underground tank constructed near or in the house/village to store harvested rainwater — traditional to Rajasthan.

    5. PMKSY: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana — "Har Khet Ko Pani" and "Per Drop More Crop."

    Every number worth having ready in your head before you open the paper.

    Non-negotiables to remember

    • Available ≠ Utilisable — 1,869 km³ is available from surface + groundwater; only 1,122 km³ (60%) is actually utilisable.
    • Domestic sector's surface-water share (9%) is HIGHER than its groundwater share (3%) — the reverse of what students often assume.
    • Yamuna is the most polluted river specifically between Delhi and Etawah — not the whole river.
    • Fluoride (Rajasthan, Maharashtra) and Arsenic (West Bengal, Bihar) are both consequences of groundwater over-withdrawal, but in different states.
    • Kund/Tanka is specifically a Rajasthan structure — do not confuse with Johad (also Rajasthan, but a dug-out pond, not underground).
    • A blind guess still carries positive expected value under CUET's marking scheme — never leave an MCQ blank.

    Mineral Types & Distribution

    • Metallic (Ferrous/Non-Ferrous) vs Non-metallic (organic/inorganic).
    • 3 belts: NE Plateau (diverse), SW Plateau (no coal), NW Region (Aravali).

    Ferrous Minerals

    • Iron ore: Haematite & Magnetite, 95% in 8 states.
    • Manganese: MP & Odisha lead.

    Non-Ferrous & Non-Metallic

    • Bauxite: Odisha leads. Copper: Singhbhum, Balaghat, Rajasthan.
    • Mica: Jharkhand/AP/Telangana/Rajasthan lead; Nellore = best quality.

    Conventional Energy

    • Jharia = largest coalfield. ONGC est. 1956. Mumbai High 1973/1976.
    • Tarapur = 1st nuclear station; Bhabha ARC renamed 1967.

    Non-Conventional Energy

    • Solar +7%/+10% vs coal-oil/nuclear. Geothermal — Manikaran (HP).
    • Bio-energy — Okhla (Delhi). Wind — Rajasthan/Gujarat/Maharashtra/Karnataka.

    Nuclear energy timeline, compact

    1948Atomic Energy Commission established
    Institute set up
    1954Atomic Energy Institute, Trombay
    Renamed

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Ferrous test

    Contains iron? Ferrous. Doesn't? Non-ferrous (copper, bauxite).

    Jharia > Raniganj

    Jharia is India's LARGEST coalfield, Raniganj is second — both in Damodar Valley.

    Bauxite exception

    India is poor in non-ferrous metals EXCEPT bauxite — Odisha leads.

    Uranium vs Thorium

    Uranium = Singhbhum copper belt + Rajasthan/Chhattisgarh/Maharashtra/HP. Thorium = Kerala/TN beach sand monazite.

    Solar's edge

    +7% vs coal/oil plants, +10% vs nuclear plants — Gujarat & Rajasthan lead potential.

    Field vs Market refinery

    Digboi = field-based (near oilfield). Barauni = market-based (near consumption).

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every formal definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 5 definitions

    1. Mineral: "a natural substance of organic or inorganic origin with definite chemical and physical properties."

    2. Ferrous minerals: minerals which have iron content (e.g. iron ore).

    3. Non-Ferrous minerals: minerals without iron content (e.g. copper, bauxite).

    4. Bauxite: the ore used in manufacturing aluminium, found in tertiary deposits associated with laterite rocks.

    5. Non-Conventional Energy: renewable, more equitably distributed and environment-friendly sources — solar, wind, hydro-geothermal, biomass.

    Planning Approaches

    • Sectoral (by sector) vs Regional (by space). NITI Aayog — 1 Jan 2015.
    • Target area (CADP, DPAP, Desert Dev, Hill Area Dev) vs Target group (SFDA, MFDA).

    DPAP & Hill Area Development

    • DPAP — Fourth Plan; 67 districts (1967); 30% irrigation criterion (1972).
    • Hill Area Dev. — Fifth Plan, 15 districts; >600m rule (1981).

    Bharmaur ITDP Case Study

    • Chamba (HP), Gaddi tribe. ITDP since 1974.
    • Female literacy: 1.88% (1971) → 65% (2011).

    Sustainable Development

    • Brundtland Report — 'Our Common Future', 1987.
    • Population Bomb (1968), Limits to Growth (1972).

    Indira Gandhi Canal Case Study

    • Conceived 1948, launched 1958. 9,060 km, 19.63 lakh ha.
    • Twin problems: waterlogging + soil salinity. 7 sustainability measures.

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Sectoral vs Regional

    Sectoral = by sector. Regional = by space, to reduce imbalance.

    NITI Aayog

    Replaced the Planning Commission on exactly 1 January 2015.

    Bharmaur's headline stat

    Female literacy: 1.88% (1971) → 65% (2011).

    Brundtland

    'Our Common Future', 1987 — the exact definition is CUET gold.

    IG Canal dates

    Conceived 1948, launched 1958 — a 10-year gap, easy to collapse into one date.

    7 measures, 5 ecological

    Only 5 of the 7 sustainability measures target ecological balance — the other 2 are social and economic.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every formal definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 5 definitions

    1. Sectoral Planning: formulation and implementation of schemes aimed at development of various sectors of the economy.

    2. Regional Planning: planning with a spatial perspective to reduce regional imbalance in development.

    3. Sustainable Development (Brundtland, 1987): "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs."

    4. Warabandi: equal distribution of canal water in the command area of an outlet.

    5. ITDP: Integrated Tribal Development Project — an area-development plan aimed at improving quality of life and narrowing the development gap.

    • Stage-I (1960s, Ganganagar belt) vs Stage-II (1980s, desert districts) of the Indira Gandhi Canal — different decades, different terrain.
    • Sustainable development is NOT purely environmental — it balances ecological, social AND economic aspects.

    2% of road length, 40% of road traffic — National Highways.

    Three gauges

    Broad = 1.676m. Metre = 1m. Narrow = 0.762/0.610m (hilly areas).

    OIL = oil pipeline, 1959, Naharkatiya-Barauni. GAIL = gas pipeline, 1984, HVJ.

    INSAT vs IRS vs PSLV

    INSAT = satellite system (1983). IRS-1A = remote-sensing satellite (1988). PSLV = the launch vehicle, not a satellite.

    1998, 760 km, Roha–Mangaluru, 146 rivers, 91 tunnels.

    Radio → TV

    Radio: 1923→1936→1957. TV: 1959 (Delhi) → 1976 (Doordarshan, delinked from AIR).

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every formal definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 4 definitions

    1. National Highways: main roads constructed and maintained by the Central Government, for inter-state transport and defence movement.

    2. National Waterways: inland waterways declared under the National Waterways Act, 2016, for development as an economical, eco-friendly transport mode.

    3. UDAN: Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik — Regional Connectivity Scheme to promote affordable regional/remote air connectivity.

    4. Personal vs Mass Communication: division of communication modes on the basis of scale and quality.

    Trade Pattern

    • Rs. 1,214cr (1950-51) → Rs. 77,19,796cr (2020-21). India ~1% of world trade.
    • Manufacturing = 67.8% of exports. Fuel = 31.6% of imports (fastest-rising).

    Direction of Trade

    • Asia+ASEAN = largest import source (₹29.19 lakh cr, 2021-22).
    • Target: double trade share in 5 years. China = main competitor.

    Sea Ports

    • 12 major + 200 minor ports. JNPT = largest container port.
    • Karachi/Chittagong lost at Partition. West coast > east coast in port count.

    Airports & Trade

    • 25 major airports (2016-17). UDAN = 73 airports since 2017.
    • 95% trade by volume / ~70% by value via ocean routes.

    India's trade growth, compact

    1950-51Rs. 1,214 crore total trade
    70 years of growth
    2020-21Rs. 77,19,796 crore total trade

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Trade growth

    Rs. 1,214cr (1950-51) → Rs. 77,19,796cr (2020-21) — yet India is still only ~1% of world trade.

    Biggest shares

    Manufacturing = 67.8% of exports. Fuel = 31.6% of imports, the fastest-rising category.

    Ports — who regulates

    Centre regulates the 12 MAJOR ports; STATES regulate the ~200 MINOR ports.

    Partition's two ports

    Karachi → Pakistan. Chittagong → Bangladesh. Replaced by Kandla and Diamond Harbour.

    Volume vs Value

    95% of trade by volume moves by sea, but only ~70% by value — air carries a disproportionate share of high-value cargo.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every formal definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 4 definitions

    1. International Trade: exchange of goods and services between countries, mutually beneficial since no country is self-sufficient.

    2. Major Ports: ports where the Central Government decides policy and plays regulatory functions.

    3. Minor Ports: ports whose policy and functions are regulated by state governments.

    4. Hinterland: the area served by a port, whose boundary is difficult to demarcate as it is not fixed over space and can overlap with neighbouring ports.

    Key Facts, Topic by Topic

    Environmental Pollution

    • 4 types: air, water, land, noise. Namami Gange = Ganga cleanup.
    • Ganga worst: Kanpur/Varanasi/Farakka. Yamuna worst: Delhi-Chambal.

    Urban Waste Disposal

    • Metros collect ~90% of waste; other towns leave 30-50% uncollected.
    • Untreated waste → methane. Swachh Bharat Mission targets slums.

    Rural-Urban Migration

    • Ramesh case study — Talcher (Odisha) to Gujarat/Maharashtra.
    • Migration stream male-dominated — low urban wages.

    Problems of Slums

    • Dharavi = Asia's largest slum, Mumbai, on reclaimed sea-land.
    • India ~69% rural (2011), yet urban areas MORE differentiated.

    Land Degradation

    • NRSC classifies wastelands. Man-made > natural degradation.
    • Jhabua (MP) case study — Bhils, Petlawad block, social fencing.

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    4 pollution types

    Air, water, land, noise — by medium of transport/diffusion.

    Ganga vs Yamuna

    Ganga worst: Kanpur, Varanasi, Farakka. Yamuna worst: Delhi to Chambal confluence.

    Male-dominated migration

    Low urban wages force families to stay behind in the village.

    Dharavi's paradox

    Asia's largest slum, reclaimed sea-land — yet produces high-value crafts.

    Degradation ≠ wasteland

    Only UNCHECKED degradation converts land to wasteland — not all degraded land qualifies.

    Jhabua

    Bhils, Petlawad block — social fencing + tree planting on Common Property Resources.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every formal definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 5 definitions

    1. Environmental Pollution: "the release of substances and energy from waste products of human activities."

    2. Water Quality issues aside, Solid Waste: old/used articles like metal pieces, glassware, plastic, ash — disposed from household and industrial/commercial sources.

    3. Slums: "residential areas of the least choice, dilapidated houses, poor hygienic conditions, poor ventilation, lack of basic amenities."

    4. Land Degradation: "a temporary or permanent decline in the productive capacity of the land."

    5. Namami Gange Programme: Union Government scheme for sewerage treatment, effluent monitoring, river-front development, afforestation and public awareness to clean the Ganga.

    Non-negotiables to remember

    • Ganga's worst stretches (Kanpur, Varanasi, Farakka) are DIFFERENT from Yamuna's worst stretch (Delhi to Chambal confluence, Mathura/Agra) — don't mix the two rivers' named locations.
    • Migration is male-dominated because of low urban wages, not because of any legal restriction on women.
    • Not all degraded land is wasteland — only unchecked, worsening degradation converts it.
    • India's urban centres are MORE differentiated than rural areas — a majority-rural country does not mean homogeneous cities.

    Key Facts, Topic by Topic

    Every load-bearing number, grouped by topic, in one scannable grid.

    Nature of Human Geography

    • 3 definitions: Ratzel, Semple, Vidal de la Blache.
    • Determinism → Possibilism → Neo-determinism (Griffith Taylor).

    Fields & Sub-fields

    • Highly inter-disciplinary — close links to social sciences.
    • Named pairs: Electoral Geography-Psephology, Population Geography-Demography.

    Three concepts, one ladder

    Environmental DeterminismNature dictates human life
    Technology improves
    PossibilismHumans exploit nature's opportunities
    Griffith Taylor's middle path
    Neo-determinismConquer nature by obeying it

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    Three definitions

    Ratzel = synthesis. Semple = dynamism. Vidal de la Blache = synthetic knowledge of physical laws + living beings.

    Benda vs Kari

    Benda (Abujh Maad) = naturalisation of humans. Kari (Trondheim) = humanisation of nature.

    Named sister-discipline pairs

    Electoral Geography↔Psephology. Population Geography↔Demography. Medical Geography↔Epidemiology.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Every formal definition from the chapter, keyword-highlighted, wording kept close to NCERT.

    Show all 3 definitions

    1. Human Geography (Ratzel): "the synthetic study of relationship between human societies and earth's surface."

    2. Human Geography (Semple): "the study of the changing relationship between the unresting man and the unstable earth."

    3. Neo-determinism (Griffith Taylor): a middle path where humans "conquer nature by obeying it."

    Non-negotiables to remember

    • Possibilism ≠ absolute freedom — Neo-determinism explicitly rejects the "free run" that caused the greenhouse effect and ozone depletion.
    • Field vs Sub-field vs Sister Discipline — three distinct columns in Table 1.2, easy to conflate.
    • A blind guess still carries positive expected value under CUET's marking scheme — never leave an MCQ blank.

    Key Facts, Topic by Topic

    Distribution & Density

    • 90% of population on 10% of land. Top 10 countries = 60% (6 in Asia).

    Population Growth

    • Grew 10× in 500 years, 4× in the 20th century alone.

    Migration

    • Push = origin repels. Pull = destination attracts.

    Demographic Transition

    • Stage I (high+high) → II (high+falling) → III (low+low). Malthus, 1798.

    Demographic transition, compact

    Stage IHigh births + high deaths (agrarian)
    Mortality falls first
    Stage IIHigh births, falling deaths (expanding)
    Fertility falls too
    Stage IIILow births + low deaths (industrial)

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    90/10 rule

    90% of world population on just 10% of its land area.

    Natural vs Actual growth

    Actual = Natural (Births−Deaths) plus net migration.

    Push vs Pull

    Push = origin problem. Pull = destination attraction.

    Stage II's real driver

    Falling MORTALITY first — fertility stays high until Stage III.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Show all 5 definitions

    1. Population Distribution: "the way people are spaced over the earth's surface."

    4. Demographic Transition: change from high births/deaths to low births/deaths as society industrialises.

    5. Malthusian Theory (1798): population grows faster than food supply, risking a population crash.

    Key Facts, Topic by Topic

    Hunting, Gathering & Pastoralism

    • Transhumance — Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis, Bhotiyas.
    • Commercial livestock: NZ, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay, USA.

    Subsistence Agriculture

    • Jhuming/Milpa/Ladang. Wet paddy = high yield/area, low yield/labour.

    Commercial Agriculture

    • Plantation = single-crop, colonial. Grain = low yield/acre, high yield/person.

    Specialized Agriculture

    • Dairy: NW Europe largest. Denmark = co-op success. Kolkhoz = Soviet collective.

    Mining

    • Began with Industrial Revolution. Surface = cheap/fast; Shaft = risky.

    All the memory tricks, in one place

    3 names, 1 practice

    Jhuming (India), Milpa (Central America), Ladang (Indonesia/Malaysia) — all shifting cultivation.

    Reversed yields

    Wet paddy = high yield/AREA, low yield/LABOUR. Extensive grain = low yield/ACRE, high yield/PERSON.

    Denmark vs Kolkhoz

    Denmark = voluntary co-operative success. Kolkhoz = Soviet state-organised collective.

    Mining's real start

    Ancient use = tools/weapons only. Real mining DEVELOPMENT = Industrial Revolution.

    All NCERT Definitions, verbatim

    Show all 5 definitions

    1. Primary Activities: directly dependent on environment — utilisation of land, water, vegetation, minerals.

    2. Transhumance: seasonal migration of pastoralists between plains and mountain pastures.

    3. Subsistence Agriculture: farming where all/nearly all produce is consumed locally.

    4. Viticulture: the cultivation of grapes, a Mediterranean speciality.

    5. Truck Farming: vegetable-only farms, named for the overnight truck-delivery range.

    Non-negotiables to remember

    • Wet paddy: high yield/AREA, low yield/LABOUR — don't reverse the two axes.
    • Extensive grain: low yield/ACRE, high yield/PERSON — the opposite reversal.
    • Nomadic herding (subsistence, unfenced) vs commercial rearing (capital-intensive, fenced) — opposite philosophies.
    • A blind guess still carries positive expected value under CUET's marking scheme — never leave an MCQ blank.

    01Distribution of Population

    India has a highly uneven pattern of population distribution — a handful of states hold the overwhelming majority of its people.

    Very high-frequency: exact % shares are a favourite MCQ trap

    NCERT Definition — Distribution of Population

    "It is clear that India has a highly uneven pattern of population distribution." Physical factors — climate, terrain and availability of water — largely determine the pattern of population distribution, together with socio-economic and historical factors such as the evolution of settled agriculture, human settlement patterns, transport development, industrialisation and urbanisation.

    Key Notes

    • Pattern is highly uneven across the country.
    • Uttar Pradesh has the highest population, followed by Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal.
    • Top 10 states together hold about 76% of India's population.
    • Smallest shares: Jammu & Kashmir (1.04%), Arunachal Pradesh (0.11%), Uttarakhand (0.84%) — despite large area.
    • Governed by physical factors (climate, terrain, water) and socio-economic factors (irrigation, minerals, transport, industry).

    The concentration

    Top of the table

    Uttar Pradesh has the highest population, followed by Maharashtra, Bihar and West Bengal. Together with Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Karnataka and Gujarat, these ten states hold about 76% of India's total population.

    Bottom of the table

    Share is very small in Jammu & Kashmir (1.04%), Arunachal Pradesh (0.11%) and Uttarakhand (0.84%) — despite fairly large geographical area.

    Characteristics — what shapes the pattern

    • Physical factors — climate, terrain and water availability. North Indian Plains, deltas and Coastal Plains carry higher population than interior southern/central districts, the Himalayas, and parts of the North-East and western states.
    • Development overrides physical limits — irrigation (Rajasthan), minerals/energy (Jharkhand), transport (Peninsular states) brought moderate-to-high concentration to previously thin areas.
    • Socio-economic & historical factors — settled agriculture, human settlement patterns, transport development, industrialisation, urbanisation.
    • River plains & coastal areas stay dense even amid resource degradation, due to early settlement history and transport links.
    • Industrial-urban belts — Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Pune, Ahmedabad, Chennai, Jaipur — high concentration from industry + rural–urban migration.

    Remember it as

    Physical factors decide the base pattern (water + climate + terrain); socio-economic factors redraw it (irrigation, minerals, transport, industry turn thin areas dense).

    02Density of Population

    Density gives a sharper, land-relative picture than raw distribution alone.

    Exact figures (382, 117, 11,297...) are asked directly almost every year

    NCERT Definition — Density of Population

    Density of population is expressed as the number of persons per unit area. It helps in getting a better understanding of the spatial distribution of population in relation to land.

    Key Notes

    • India's density: 382/km² (2011), up from 117/km² (1951).
    • Highest: NCT of Delhi (11,297/km²). Lowest: Arunachal Pradesh (17/km²).
    • Among major states: Bihar (1,102) and West Bengal (1,029) highest; Kerala (859) and Uttar Pradesh (828) next.
    • Physiological Density = Population ÷ Net Cultivated Area — a sharper measure than crude density.
    • Agricultural Density = Agricultural Population ÷ Net Cultivable Area.

    NCT of Delhi (11,297/km², the highest in India) is left out of the chart above on purpose — at that scale it would dwarf every other bar. Moderate density: Assam, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Jharkhand, Odisha. Low: Himalayan hill states & North-East (excl. Assam). Very high: Union Territories (excl. Andaman & Nicobar).

    Beyond crude density

    Physiological Density = Total Population ÷ Net Cultivated Area
    Agricultural Density = Total Agricultural Population ÷ Net Cultivable Area

    Definition — Agricultural Population

    Cultivators and agricultural labourers, and their family members.

    Remember it as

    Plain density = people ÷ all land. Physiological density = people ÷ farmed land — a truer pressure-on-agriculture measure, since crude density is "a crude measure of human and land relationship."

    03Growth of Population

    Growth is the change in the number of people in an area between two points in time, expressed as a percentage.

    The single most-tested topic in this chapter — phases, formula, and Table 1.1

    NCERT Definition — Two components

    Natural growth is assessed via crude birth and death rates. Induced growth comes from migration. This chapter covers only natural growth.

    NCERT Definition — Doubling Time

    The time taken by any population to double itself at its current annual growth rate.

    Key Notes

    • Annual growth rate (2011): 1.64%. Decadal growth (2001–11): 17.64%.
    • Only negative decade: 1911–1921 (−0.31%).
    • Four phases: Stagnant (1901–21) → Steady (1921–51) → Explosion (1951–81) → Slowdown (1981–present).
    • Projected population by 2025: 1,350 million (World Development Report).

    Formula

    Decadal Growth Rate (g) = [ (P₂ − P₁) ÷ P₁ ] × 100

    Table 1.1 — Decadal Growth Rates, 1901–2011

    YearPopulation% Growth
    190123,83,96,327—
    191125,20,93,390(+) 5.75
    192125,13,21,213(−) 0.31
    193127,89,77,238(+) 11.60
    194131,86,60,580(+) 14.22
    195136,10,88,090(+) 13.31
    196143,92,34,771(+) 21.51
    197154,81,59,652(+) 24.80
    198168,33,29,097(+) 24.66
    199184,63,02,688(+) 23.85
    20011,02,86,10,328(+) 21.54
    20111,21,01,93,422(+) 17.64

    Source: Census of India, 2011 (Provisional). The only negative decade: 1911–1921.

    The four phases — characteristics

    • Phase I — Stagnant (1901–1921): very low growth, negative during 1911–1921. Both birth and death rates high. Cause: poor health/medical services, illiteracy, inefficient food distribution.
    • Phase II — Steady Growth (1921–1951): improved health & sanitation cut mortality; better transport/communication improved distribution. Birth rate stayed high, so growth exceeded Phase I — despite the Great Depression and WWII.
    • Phase III — Population Explosion (1951–1981): mortality fell rapidly while fertility stayed high; average annual growth as high as 2.2%. Post-Independence planning improved living conditions; international migration (Tibetans, Bangladeshis, Nepalis, Pakistanis) also contributed.
    • Phase IV — Slowing Growth (1981–present): still high but slowing gradually, due to a falling crude birth rate — driven by rising age at marriage and improved female education.

    Remember it as

    Stagnant → Steady → Explosion → Slowdown. Phase I: both rates high. Phase II: deaths fall, births stay high. Phase III: deaths crash, births still high → explosion. Phase IV: births finally start falling too.

    Classify the decade — which phase?

    1911–1921 (negative growth)

    Phase I — the stagnant phase, with growth even turning negative in this decade.

    1961–1971 (24.80% growth)

    Phase III — the population explosion (1951–1981), averaging 2.2%/year.

    2001–2011 (17.64%, falling)

    Phase IV — growth is high but gradually slowing, due to a falling birth rate.

    04Regional Variation in Population Growth

    The national average hides wide state-to-state variation.

    Kerala's 9.4% is the most commonly quoted single figure from this section

    NCERT Definition — Regional Variation in Growth

    "The growth rate of population during 1991–2001 in Indian States and Union Territories shows [a] very obvious pattern" — splitting the country into a low-growth south and a high-growth northern belt.

    Key Notes

    • Low growth (under 20%, 1991–2001): Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Puducherry, Goa. Kerala's 9.4% was the lowest in the country.
    • High-growth belt (20–25%): Gujarat, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, UP, Uttarakhand, MP, Sikkim, Assam, WB, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand.
    • 2001–11: growth fell almost everywhere; Maharashtra fell most (−6.7 pts); Tamil Nadu (+3.9) and Puducherry (+7.1) rose instead.

    05Adolescent Population

    India's youth bulge is both an opportunity and a policy challenge.

    NCERT Definition — Adolescent Population

    "An important aspect of population growth in India is the growth of its adolescents" — the share of population "up to the age group of 10–19 years."

    Key Notes

    • Adolescents = 20.9% of population (2011) — 52.7% male, 47.3% female.
    • National Youth Policy (NYP–2014) defines 'youth' as 15–29 years — a different band from "adolescents."
    • National Policy for Skill Development & Entrepreneurship — 2015.
    Adolescents (10–19 yrs)20.9% of population

    — Female adolescents47.3%

    Challenges

    • Lower age at marriage · Illiteracy (especially female) · School dropouts
    • Low nutrient intake · High maternal mortality among adolescent mothers
    • High HIV/AIDS rates · Physical & mental disability
    • Drug abuse and alcoholism · Juvenile delinquency

    Policy response

    National Youth Policy (NYP–2014) Feb 2014

    Vision: "To empower the youth of the country to achieve their full potential, and through them enable India to find its rightful place in the community of nations." Defines 'youth' as 15–29 years.

    06Population Composition — Rural–Urban

    Over two-thirds of India still lives in villages — but the urban share is growing fastest.

    68.8% / 31.16% split is asked directly and via comparison MCQs

    NCERT Definition — Rural–Urban Composition

    "Composition of population by their respective places of residence is an important indicator of social and economic characteristics."

    Key Notes

    • 68.8% rural, 31.16% urban (2011).
    • 6,40,867 villages in India; 93.2% (5,97,608) are inhabited.
    • Very high rural share: Himachal Pradesh, Bihar. Close to half urban: Goa, Mizoram.
    • Urban growth driven by economic development and rural–urban migration along industrial corridors.
    Rural68.8%
    Urban31.16%

    Villages — inhabited share

    Total villages6,40,867
    Inhabited villages5,97,608 (93.2%)

    Rural — characteristics

    • Very high rural share: Himachal Pradesh, Bihar. Only ~half rural: Goa, Mizoram.
    • UTs mostly have a smaller rural share — except Dadra & Nagar Haveli (53.38%).
    • Village size ranges from under 200 persons (NE hill states, Western Rajasthan, Rann of Kuchchh) to 17,000 persons (parts of Kerala, Maharashtra).
    • India has 6,40,867 villages; 93.2% (5,97,608) are inhabited.

    Urban — characteristics

    • Low proportion but growing much faster — driven by economic development, better health/hygiene.
    • Migration hot-spots: North Indian Plains corridors; industrial belts around Kolkata, Mumbai, Bengaluru–Mysuru, Madurai–Coimbatore, Ahmedabad–Surat, Delhi–Kanpur, Ludhiana–Jalandhar.

    07Population Composition — Linguistic

    India's language regions blur into each other rather than snap to hard borders.

    Table 1.2's 4 families & their % shares are a recurring MCQ/match-the-following theme

    Key Notes

    • 4 language families: Indo-European (73%), Dravidian (20%), Austric (1.38%), Sino-Tibetan (0.85%).
    • Highest speaker share: Hindi. Smallest scheduled groups (2011): Sanskrit, Bodo, Manipuri.
    • Linguistic regions do not have sharp boundaries — they merge and overlap at frontier zones.

    Interactive Key Points — tap each card to reveal

    Test yourself before you look — tap a card to see if you guessed right.

    Which language family has the largest share of speakers?

    Indo-European (Aryan) — 73% of India's speakers. Includes Indo-Aryan, Dardic and Iranian sub-families.

    Which family comes second, with about a fifth of speakers?

    Dravidian — 20%, spread across South, Central and North Dravidian branches (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, and more).

    How many languages and dialects did Grierson's Linguistic Survey (1903–28) record?

    179 languages and as many as 544 dialects.

    Which is the highest-speaker scheduled language in India?

    Hindi — the highest percentage among scheduled languages.

    Which are the smallest scheduled-language groups (2011)?

    Sanskrit, Bodo and Manipuri speakers.

    Do India's linguistic regions have sharp, clearly defined boundaries?

    No — they gradually merge and overlap at their frontier zones, rather than snapping to a hard border.

    Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India, 1903–1928

    Recorded 179 languages and 544 dialects. Modern India recognises about 22 scheduled languages.

    01Human Settlements — Meaning & Types

    A settlement can be a single hamlet or a metropolis of millions — but the line between "rural" and "urban" is drawn by what its people do for a living, not just how many of them there are.

    Foundational definitions — a frequent one-line MCQ source

    NCERT Definition — Human Settlement

    "Human Settlement means cluster of dwellings of any type or size where human beings live." The process of settlement inherently involves grouping of people and apportioning of territory as their resource base.

    Key Notes

    • Settlements range from a hamlet to a metropolitan city.
    • Small, sparsely spaced settlements are villages — specialising in agriculture / other primary activities.
    • Fewer but larger settlements are urban settlements — specialising in secondary and tertiary activities.
    • With size, a settlement's economic character, social structure, ecology and technology all change.

    Rural vs Urban — the three basic differences

    BasisRural settlementsUrban settlements
    Economic baseLand-based primary economic activitiesProcessing of raw materials, manufacturing of finished goods, and a variety of services
    Functional roleSupply food and raw materials to cities, via their hinterlandsAct as nodes of economic growth; supply goods & services to both urban dwellers and rural hinterlands, connected through transport & communication
    Social relationsLess mobile; relations are intimateWay of life is complex and fast; relations are formal

    This functional relationship between rural and urban settlements — goods and services flowing one way, food and raw materials the other — runs through the transport and communication network.

    Sort the characteristic — rural or urban?

    Life support from land-based primary activities

    Rural settlements derive their basic economic needs from land-based primary activities.

    Acts as a node of economic growth

    Cities act as nodes of economic growth, providing goods and services to their rural hinterlands.

    Social relations are intimate; people are less mobile

    Rural people are less mobile, so social relations among them stay intimate.

    Depends on processing raw materials and manufacturing finished goods

    Urban settlements depend on processing and manufacturing, plus a variety of services.

    Remember it as

    Rural = land feeds you; Urban = factories and services employ you. The two stay connected because cities need rural food and raw materials, and villages need urban goods and services.

    02Types of Rural Settlement

    The same open countryside produces four very different-looking villages, depending on terrain, culture and safety.

    The single most-tested topic in this chapter — matching type ↔ region is a recurring MCQ

    NCERT Definition — What determines settlement type

    "Types of the settlement are determined by the extent of the built-up area and inter-house distance." In India, a compact or clustered village of a few hundred houses is a "rather universal feature," particularly in the northern plains.

    Key Notes

    • Rural settlements in India fall into four broad types: Clustered, Semi-Clustered, Hamleted, Dispersed.
    • Three groups of factors decide the type: physical (terrain, altitude, climate, water) · cultural/ethnic (social structure, caste, religion) · security (defence against theft and robbery).

    The four types

    • Clustered (agglomerated / nucleated): a compact, closely built-up area of houses, distinct from the surrounding farms, barns and pastures — often in a recognisable geometric shape (rectangular, radial, linear). Found in fertile alluvial plains and the north-eastern states; also for security/defence (Bundelkhand, Nagaland) and to maximise scarce water use (Rajasthan).
    • Semi-Clustered (fragmented): clustering in a restricted area of an otherwise dispersed settlement, often from segregation of a large compact village — the land-owning/dominant community occupies the centre, lower-strata and menial workers settle on the outer flanks. Widespread in the Gujarat plain and parts of Rajasthan.
    • Hamleted: fragmented into several separated units sharing one common name — locally called panna, para, palli, nagla, dhani, etc. — usually from social/ethnic segmentation. Common in the middle and lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh and lower Himalayan valleys.
    • Dispersed (isolated): isolated huts or tiny hamlets in remote jungles or on small hills with farms/pasture on the slopes, caused by extremely fragmented terrain and habitable land. Found in Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Kerala.

    Type ↔ region — visualised

    TypeWhere it's typically foundWhy
    ClusteredNorthern plains, NE states, Bundelkhand, Nagaland, RajasthanFertile alluvium; defence; scarce water needs maximum shared use
    Semi-ClusteredGujarat plain, parts of RajasthanSegregation/fragmentation of a large compact village
    HamletedMiddle/lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh, lower Himalayan valleysSocial and ethnic segmentation
    DispersedMeghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, KeralaExtremely fragmented terrain and habitable land

    Which type — classify each clue

    Compact village, geometric street pattern, northern plains

    Clustered settlements form a compact, closely built-up area with a recognisable shape — the "universal feature" of the northern plains.

    Dominant community at the centre, lower-strata workers on the outer flanks, Gujarat plain

    This centre/flank social segregation pattern, widespread in the Gujarat plain, defines Semi-Clustered settlements.

    Several separated units sharing one common name — panna, para, palli, nagla, dhani

    These locally-named separated units are the defining feature of Hamleted settlements.

    Isolated huts in remote jungle, extremely fragmented terrain, Meghalaya

    Isolated huts scattered by extremely fragmented terrain define the Dispersed type.

    Remember it as

    Clustered = compact & together. Semi-clustered = together, but split by class. Hamleted = split into several named pieces. Dispersed = scattered, isolated huts. The driver is always one of: physical terrain, cultural/ethnic divide, or security.

    03Urban Settlements — Census Definition

    India's census draws a precise, three-part line between a "town" and a village — and CUET loves testing the exact numbers.

    The 5,000 / 75% / 400 figures are asked directly almost every cycle

    NCERT Definition — Urban Settlement (Census of India, 1991)

    "All places which have municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee and have a minimum population of 5,000 persons, at least 75 per cent of male workers are engaged in non-agriculture pursuits and a density of population of at least 400 persons per square kilometre are urban."

    Key Notes

    • Urban settlements are compact and larger in size than rural ones, engaged in non-agricultural, economic and administrative functions.
    • Cities are functionally linked to rural areas around them — exchange of goods/services happens directly, or through a series of market towns in between.
    • All three numeric thresholds — population, worker composition, density — must be met together with the administrative-status condition.

    The four-part test — visualised

    5,000+
    Minimum population
    75%+
    Male workers in non-agriculture
    400+/km²
    Minimum population density

    Plus — administrative status

    The place must also have a municipality, corporation, cantonment board, or notified town area committee — the four qualifying local-government forms.

    Spot the missing/wrong criterion

    "At least 75% of male workers engaged in agriculture"

    The Census definition requires 75%+ of male workers in NON-agriculture, the opposite of this statement.

    "Minimum population density of 400 persons per sq km"

    Correct — 400 persons/km² is exactly the Census threshold.

    "Minimum population of 10,000 persons"

    The actual threshold is 5,000 persons, not 10,000.

    Remember it as

    5 / 75 / 400 — population of at least 5,000, at least 75% of male workers in non-agriculture, and a density of at least 400 persons/km² — plus a municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee.

    04Evolution of Towns in India

    India's towns carry the fingerprints of three very different eras — ancient, medieval, and colonial-modern.

    Matching towns to their era (Ancient/Medieval/Modern) is a classic MCQ trap

    NCERT Definition — Basis of Classification

    Towns "flourished since prehistoric times" — even the Indus Valley Civilisation had towns like Harappa and Mohenjodaro. Evolution continued with ups and downs until Europeans arrived, in the eighteenth century. On the basis of their evolution in different periods, Indian towns are classified as Ancient, Medieval and Modern.

    Three eras

    • Ancient towns — historical background spanning over 2,000 years; mostly developed as religious and cultural centres. Examples: Varanasi, Prayag (Prayagraj), Pataliputra (Patna), Madurai.
    • Medieval towns — about 100 of today's towns are rooted here; mostly headquarters of principalities/kingdoms — fort towns built on the ruins of ancient towns. Examples: Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Agra, Nagpur.
    • Modern towns — developed by the British and other Europeans. Began as coastal trading ports (Surat, Daman, Goa, Pondicherry), then consolidated around three principal nodes — Mumbai (Bombay), Chennai (Madras), Kolkata (Calcutta) — built in British style, plus hill-towns as summer resorts. Industrial modern towns evolved after 1850 (e.g. Jamshedpur).

    Evolution — visualised

    Ancient2,000+ yrs · religious/cultural centres
    Fort towns rise on their ruins
    Medieval~100 towns · principality/kingdom HQs
    Europeans arrive, 18th century
    ModernCoastal ports → 3 nodes → post-1850 industry

    After Independence

    • Administrative headquarters: Chandigarh, Bhubaneswar, Gandhinagar, Dispur.
    • Industrial centres: Durgapur, Bhilai, Sindri, Barauni.
    • Satellite towns around metros: Ghaziabad, Rohtak, Gurugram — all around Delhi.

    Remember it as

    Ancient = religion (Varanasi, Madurai). Medieval = forts & kingdoms (Delhi, Jaipur, Agra). Modern = the British — three nodes: Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata.

    05Urbanisation in India

    India is urbanising — just far more slowly than most developed countries, and the pace has cooled further in the last two decades.

    Table 2.1's 2011 figures (6,171 towns, 31.16%) are asked almost every cycle

    NCERT Definition — Level of Urbanisation

    The level of urbanisation is measured "in terms of percentage of urban population to total population." India's level of urbanisation in 2011 was 31.16 per cent — quite low compared to developed countries.

    Key Notes

    • Total urban population increased eleven-fold during the twentieth century.
    • Enlargement of existing urban centres and emergence of new towns both drove this growth.
    • The decennial growth rate of the urban population has slowed down over the last two decades — even though the urban share keeps rising.

    NCERT context — even after eleven-fold growth in the twentieth century, India's urbanisation level remains well below that of most developed countries.

    06Functional Classification of Towns

    Every town does a bit of everything — but most are still best known for the one function that put them on the map.

    Matching a named town to its function is the single most common question type from this chapter

    NCERT Definition — Functional Classification

    "On the basis of dominant or specialised functions, Indian cities and towns can be broadly classified" into nine functional categories. But "each town performs a number of functions" — the classification reflects the dominant one.

    The nine functional classes

    ClassExamples (as named by NCERT)
    AdministrativeChandigarh, New Delhi, Bhopal, Shillong, Guwahati, Imphal, Srinagar, Gandhinagar, Jaipur, Chennai
    IndustrialMumbai, Salem, Coimbatore, Modinagar, Jamshedpur, Hugli, Bhilai
    TransportPorts: Kandla, Cochin, Kozhikode, Vishakhapatnam · Inland hubs: Agra, Dhulia, Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Nagar, Itarsi, Katni
    CommercialKolkata, Saharanpur, Satna
    MiningRaniganj, Jharia, Digboi, Ankaleshwar, Singrauli
    Garrison CantonmentAmbala, Jalandhar, Mhow, Babina, Udhampur
    EducationalRoorki, Varanasi, Aligarh, Pilani, Prayagraj
    Religious & CulturalVaranasi, Mathura, Amritsar, Madurai, Puri, Ajmer, Pushkar, Tirupati, Kurukshetra, Haridwar, Ujjain
    TouristNainital, Mussoorie, Shimla, Pachmarhi, Jodhpur, Jaisalmer, Udagamandalam (Ooty), Mount Abu

    Notice Varanasi appears in BOTH Educational and Religious & Cultural — a reminder that "dominant function" isn't the only function a town performs.

    Smart Cities Mission

    Objective: promote cities that provide core infrastructure, a clean and sustainable environment, and a decent quality of life — via smart solutions (less disaster-vulnerable, fewer resources, cheaper services). Focus: sustainable and inclusive development, starting from compact areas as a replicable model — "a lighthouse to other aspiring cities."

    Which function?

    Chandigarh, Gandhinagar, Bhopal

    All three are administrative headquarters — Administrative towns.

    Raniganj, Jharia, Digboi

    Developed in mineral-rich areas — Mining towns.

    Ambala, Jalandhar, Mhow

    These emerged as garrison towns — Garrison Cantonment towns.

    Nainital, Mussoorie, Shimla

    Hill-station tourist destinations — Tourist towns.

    Remember it as

    Cities are dynamic, not static — as a specialised town grows into a metropolis, industry, business, administration and transport all get intertwined, and it stops fitting any single functional box.

    01Land Use Categories & Changes

    Every hectare of India's reporting area is sorted into one of nine land-use categories — and how those categories have shifted since 1950 tells its own story.

    Identifying which categories rose vs fell (1950-51→2019-20) is a recurring MCQ

    NCERT Definition — Land-Use Categories

    Land-use records are maintained by the land revenue department. The land-use categories add up to reporting area, which is different from geographical area (measured by the Survey of India, which stays fixed).

    Key Notes

    • Nine categories: Forests, Barren & Wastelands, Non-agricultural Uses, Permanent Pastures & Grazing Lands, Misc. Tree Crops & Groves, Culturable Wasteland, Current Fallow, Fallow other than Current, Net Area Sown.
    • An increase in "forest" area often reflects more land demarcated for forest growth, not more actual forest cover.
    • Culturable wasteland = fallow for more than 5 years. Fallow other than current = uncultivated 1–5 years. Current fallow = uncultivated for ≤1 year.

    The nine categories

    CategoryWhat it means
    ForestsArea demarcated for forest growth — different from actual forest cover
    Barren & WastelandsBarren hilly terrain, deserts, ravines — can't be cultivated with available technology
    Non-agricultural UsesSettlements, infrastructure, industries, shops
    Permanent Pastures & Grazing LandsMostly owned by the village Panchayat or Government
    Misc. Tree Crops & GrovesOrchards and fruit trees, mostly privately owned; not part of Net Sown Area
    Culturable WastelandLeft fallow for more than 5 years
    Current FallowUncultivated for one year or less
    Fallow other than CurrentUncultivated for more than 1 but less than 5 years
    Net Area SownPhysical extent of land on which crops are actually sown and harvested

    1950–51 → 2019–20: what rose, what fell

    • Rose: Forests, Non-agricultural uses (fastest-rising), Permanent pasture & grazing land, Current fallow, Net area sown.
    • Fell: Barren & wasteland, Culturable wasteland, Area under tree crops & groves, Fallow other than current fallow.
    • Non-agricultural use rose fastest — driven by industry, services, and expanding urban/rural settlements, eating into wasteland and agricultural land.
    • Net sown area's recent rise comes from culturable wasteland being brought under the plough — before that, it was slowly declining (lost mostly to non-agricultural use).

    Which direction — up or down since 1950-51?

    Area under non-agricultural uses

    Increased — the fastest-rising category, driven by industry, services and settlement expansion.

    Culturable wasteland

    Decreased — pressure from both agricultural and non-agricultural sectors reduced wastelands over time.

    Net area sown

    Increased (recently) — culturable wasteland has been brought under cultivation.

    Area under tree crops and groves

    Decreased — squeezed out by pressure from agricultural land.

    Remember it as

    5 up, 4 down. Up: Forests, Non-agri use, Pasture, Current fallow, Net sown. Down: Barren/waste, Culturable waste, Tree crops/groves, Fallow-other-than-current.

    02Common Property Resources & Agricultural Land

    Not all land is privately owned — common property resources keep landless and marginal farmers afloat, while India's total stock of cultivable land has been quietly shrinking.

    NCERT Definition — Common Property Resources (CPRs)

    CPRs are a community's natural resource, where every member has the right of access and usage with specified obligations, without anybody having property rights over them. Community forests, pasture lands and village water bodies are examples.

    Key Notes

    • Land is either private (individual/group-owned) or CPR (state-owned, for community use).
    • CPRs provide fodder for livestock and fuel for households, plus fruits, nuts, fibre, medicinal plants.
    • Especially important for women (who mostly collect fodder/fuel) and the landless/marginal farmers who depend on livestock income.
    • Total cultivable land = Net Sown Area + all Fallow lands + Culturable Wasteland.

    Table 3.1 — Composition of Total Cultivable Land (% of Reporting Area)

    Category1950–512019–20
    Culturable Wasteland8.0%3.9%
    Fallow other than Current Fallow6.1%3.7%
    Current Fallow3.7%4.5%
    Net Area Sown41.7%45.6%
    Total Cultivable Land59.5%57.7%

    Total cultivable land has slipped only slightly (59.5% → 57.7%) — but within it, Net Area Sown has grown while both wasteland and fallow categories have shrunk.

    Total cultivable land — visualised

    1950–5159.5%
    2019–2057.7%

    Why land matters more to agriculture than to other sectors

    • Agriculture is purely land-based — unlike secondary/tertiary activities, land's contribution to output is much higher.
    • Quality of land directly affects agricultural productivity, unlike most other activities.
    • In rural areas, land ownership has social value too — security for credit, protection against hazards, and social status.

    Remember it as

    CPR = community-owned, no one's private property — vital for the landless. Total cultivable land = Net Sown + all Fallow + Culturable Wasteland.

    03Cropping Seasons & Types of Farming

    India's crop calendar runs on three seasons in the north — but the south barely slows down at all.

    Table 3.2's Kharif/Rabi/Zaid crop lists are asked almost every cycle

    NCERT Definition — Cropping Intensity

    Cropping Intensity (CI) = (Gross Cropped Area ÷ Net Sown Area) × 100. A high cropping intensity means fuller utilisation of land — valuable for a "land scarce but labour abundant" country like India.

    Key Notes

    • Three seasons in northern/interior India: Kharif (with SW Monsoon), Rabi (Oct–Nov to Mar–Apr, winter), Zaid (short summer season after Rabi harvest).
    • In southern India, temperature stays high enough to grow tropical crops any time of year — the same crop can be grown thrice a year given enough soil moisture.
    • Farming types: Irrigated (protective vs productive) and Rainfed/Barani (dryland vs wetland).
    Cropping Intensity (%) = (Gross Cropped Area ÷ Net Sown Area) × 100

    Table 3.2 — Cropping Seasons in India

    SeasonNorthern StatesSouthern States
    Kharif
    (June–September)    		Rice, Cotton, Bajra, Maize, Jowar, TurRice, Maize, Ragi, Jowar, Groundnut
    Rabi
    (October–March)    		Wheat, Gram, Rapeseeds and Mustard, BarleyRice, Maize, Ragi, Groundnut, Jowar
    Zaid
    (April–June)    		Vegetables, Fruits, FodderRice, Vegetables, Fodder

    Farming types

    • Protective irrigation: supplements rainfall to protect crops from moisture deficiency, spread over maximum possible area.
    • Productive irrigation: supplies sufficient soil moisture for high productivity — higher water input per unit area.
    • Dryland farming: confined to regions with <75 cm annual rainfall — hardy, drought-resistant crops (ragi, bajra, moong, gram, guar).
    • Wetland farming: rainfall exceeds plant moisture needs — water-intensive crops (rice, jute, sugarcane); risk of flood/soil erosion.

    Which season — Kharif, Rabi or Zaid?

    Coincides with the Southwest Monsoon — rice, cotton, jute

    Kharif — largely coincides with the Southwest Monsoon.

    Begins with onset of winter, Oct–Nov to Mar–Apr — wheat, gram, mustard

    Rabi — the winter cropping season.

    Short summer season after Rabi harvest — watermelons, cucumbers

    Zaid — a short-duration summer season on irrigated land.

    Remember it as

    Kharif = monsoon-sown. Rabi = winter-sown. Zaid = short summer gap-filler. In the south, seasons blur — the same crop can grow three times a year.

    04Foodgrains — Cereals

    Foodgrains occupy about two-thirds of India's total cropped area — and cereals alone make up the majority of that.

    Rice and wheat's exact % of cropped area and leading states are asked almost every cycle

    NCERT Definition — Foodgrains

    Foodgrains occupy about two-thirds of the total cropped area in India, and are dominant in both subsistence and commercial agricultural economies. Based on grain structure, foodgrains are classed as cereals and pulses.

    Key Notes

    • Cereals = ~54% of total cropped area; India produces ~11% of world cereals, ranking 3rd after China and USA.
    • Fine grains: rice, wheat. Coarse grains: jowar, bajra, maize, ragi.
    • Rice: ~22.07% of world production, 2nd after China (2018); ~¼ of India's cropped area; leading states West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Punjab.
    • Wheat: ~12.8% of world production; ~14% of cropped area; ~85% concentrated in north/central India; leading state Uttar Pradesh.

    Share of total cropped area — visualised

    Rice~25%
    Wheat~14%
    Jowar~5.3%
    Bajra~5.2%
    Maize~3.6%

    Scaled to rice's ~25% = 100%. All coarse cereals (jowar+bajra+maize+ragi) together make up ~16.5% of cropped area.

    The major cereals

    • Rice: Punjab, Haryana grow it under irrigation (introduced 1970s, post-Green Revolution — not traditional rice areas). Very low yield in rainfed MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha. West Bengal grows 3 crops/year: aus, aman, boro.
    • Wheat: a rabi crop, mostly irrigated; rainfed in Himalayan highlands & Malwa plateau. Very high yield (>4,000 kg/ha) in Punjab, Haryana.
    • Jowar: main food crop of semi-arid central/south India; Maharashtra produces >half of national output.
    • Bajra: hardy, drought-resistant; hot/dry NW & western India; leading state Rajasthan.
    • Maize: food + fodder crop, grown nearly everywhere except Punjab and the NE; highest yield in southern states.

    Remember it as

    Rice = wet & irrigated (WB, UP, Punjab). Wheat = rabi & irrigated (UP leads). Jowar/Bajra/Maize = coarse, drought-tolerant, together barely beat wheat's share alone.

    05Pulses and Oilseeds

    Protein and oil — grown mostly on the rainfed drylands other crops can't use.

    NCERT Definition — Pulses

    Pulses are legume crops which increase the natural fertility of soils through nitrogen fixation. India is a leading producer of pulses in the world.

    Key Notes

    • Pulses = ~11% of cropped area; concentrated in drylands of the Deccan, central plateaus, and NW India. Gram and Tur are the main pulses.
    • Oilseeds = ~14% of cropped area; main crops: groundnut, rapeseed & mustard, soyabean, sunflower.
    • Groundnut: ~18.8% of world production (2018); mostly rainfed kharif crop of drylands; leading state Gujarat.
    • Rapeseed & Mustard: rabi, frost-sensitive; ~⅔ of area irrigated; Rajasthan contributes ~⅓ of production.

    Share of total cropped area — visualised

    Pulses (all)~11%
    Oilseeds (all)~14%
    — Groundnut~3.6%
    — Rapeseed & Mustard~2.5%
    — Gram~2.8%
    — Tur (Arhar)~2%

    Pulses

    • Gram: mostly rainfed, rabi, subtropical; displaced by wheat in Haryana/Punjab/N. Rajasthan post-Green Revolution. Main producer: Madhya Pradesh.
    • Tur (Arhar / red gram / pigeon pea): grown on marginal, rainfed land in central/southern drylands. Maharashtra ~⅓ of national output.

    Oilseeds

    • Soyabean: Madhya Pradesh + Maharashtra = ~90% of national output.
    • Sunflower: Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, adjoining Maharashtra; a minor but high-yield crop in irrigated north India.

    Remember it as

    Pulses fix nitrogen — good for soil, low yield, rainfed drylands. Oilseeds are for edible oil — Groundnut (kharif), Rapeseed/Mustard (rabi) are the two biggest by area.

    06Fibre & Plantation Crops

    Cotton, jute, sugarcane, tea and coffee — the crops India grows to sell, not just to eat.

    State-wise production leaders (Assam=tea, WB=jute, UP=sugarcane) are a classic match-the-following theme

    NCERT Definition — Fibre Crops
