    Fibre crops provide fibre for cloth, bags, sacks and other items. Cotton and jute are the two main fibre crops grown in India.

    Key Notes

    • Cotton: kharif, semi-arid, India ranks 2nd in the world after China; ~4.7% of cropped area; 3 growing belts — NW (Punjab/Haryana/Rajasthan), West (Gujarat/Maharashtra), South (AP/Karnataka/TN).
    • Jute: West Bengal produces ~¾ of national output; India makes ~⅗ of world jute; only ~0.5% of cropped area.
    • Sugarcane: India 2nd after Brazil (~19.7% of world output, 2018); Uttar Pradesh grows ~⅖ of national output; only ~2.4% of cropped area.
    • Tea: Assam ~53.2% of national output; started 1840s in Brahmaputra valley. Coffee: mostly arabica; Karnataka >⅔ of national output.

    Top state's share of national output — visualised

    Jute — West Bengal~75%
    Coffee — Karnataka>67%
    Tea — Assam53.2%
    Sugarcane — Uttar Pradesh~40%

    Crop ↔ leading state

    Tea — accounts for over half of India's production

    Assam contributes more than half of India's tea production (53.2%).

    Jute — about three-fourths of national output

    West Bengal accounts for about three-fourths of India's jute production.

    Sugarcane — about two-fifths of national output

    Uttar Pradesh produces about two-fifths of India's sugarcane.

    Remember it as

    Assam = tea. West Bengal = jute. Uttar Pradesh = sugarcane. Karnataka = coffee. Each state dominates its crop by 40–75% of national output.

    07Agricultural Development in India

    From famine-prone subsistence farming to the Green Revolution that made India self-reliant in foodgrains.

    The Green Revolution's origin states and timeline are a favourite MCQ

    NCERT Definition — The Green Revolution

    New High Yielding Varieties (HYVs) of wheat (from Mexico) and rice (from the Philippines) became available by mid-1960s. India adopted this package technology — HYVs plus chemical fertilisers — in irrigated areas, sparking the "Green Revolution."

    Key Notes

    • Pre-Independence: agriculture was largely subsistence; the first half of the 20th century saw severe droughts and famines.
    • Partition sent about ⅓ of undivided India's irrigated land to Pakistan.
    • Green Revolution started in Punjab, Haryana, Western UP, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat — initially confined to irrigated areas, causing regional disparities until it spread to eastern/central India after the 1970s.
    • Agro-climatic planning began in 1988; liberalisation/free market policy from 1990s.
    • Chemical fertiliser use rose 15× since the mid-1960s.

    Timeline — visualised

    Pre-1947Subsistence, droughts, famines
    IADP, IAAP launched; droughts persist
    Mid-1960sHYV seeds arrive — Green Revolution begins
    Spreads to eastern/central India post-1970s
    1988 onwardAgro-climatic planning, diversification, liberalisation (1990s)

    Post-Independence strategy (immediate goals)

    • Switching from cash crops to food crops.
    • Intensification of cropping over already-cultivated land.
    • Increasing cultivated area by bringing cultivable/fallow land under the plough.
    • Production stagnated late-1950s → IADP & IAAP launched → two consecutive droughts, mid-1960s → food imports.

    National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA)

    Aims to make agriculture more productive, sustainable, remunerative and climate resilient. Promotes organic farming via Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY) and Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana (RKVY).

    Remember it as

    Green Revolution = HYV seed + irrigation + fertiliser, born in Punjab/Haryana/W.UP, mid-1960s — initially unequal, later spread everywhere.

    08Problems of Indian Agriculture

    Bigger harvests haven't solved agriculture's oldest problems — they've just changed their shape.

    NCERT Definition — Degradation of Cultivable Land

    Faulty irrigation and agricultural strategy have caused degradation of land resources — especially in irrigated areas, through alkalisation, salinisation and waterlogging.

    Key Notes

    • Irrigation covers only ~33% of cultivated area — the rest depends directly on the monsoon.
    • Yields lag behind the USA, Russia and Japan for rice, wheat, cotton, oilseeds.
    • Among the 3 British-era revenue systems (Mahalwari, Ryotwari, Zamindari), Zamindari was most exploitative.
    • Seasonal unemployment in unirrigated tracts can run 4–8 months a year.

    Seven recurring problems

    • Dependence on erratic monsoon: poor SW monsoon hits canal-irrigation too; Rajasthan/drought-prone areas get meagre, unreliable rain; even high-rainfall areas see big swings, risking both drought and flood.
    • Low productivity: per-hectare output lags the USA/Russia/Japan; labour productivity is also low due to high pressure on land.
    • Financial constraints & indebtedness: modern inputs are expensive; small/marginal farmers borrow from institutions and moneylenders, and crop failure traps them in debt.
    • Lack of land reforms: unequal land distribution persisted post-Independence due to weak political will against landlord lobbies.
    • Small farm size & fragmentation: holdings shrink under population pressure and fragment further across generations.
    • Lack of commercialisation: many small/marginal farmers grow only enough foodgrain for their own family.
    • Vast underemployment: especially in unirrigated tracts — 4 to 8 months of seasonal unemployment.

    Land degradation — the mechanisms

    • Irrigated areas: alkalisation and salinisation of soils, waterlogging; excess pesticide/insecticide use leaves toxic residues; multiple cropping has cut fallow duration, weakening natural nitrogen fixation.
    • Rainfed areas (humid/semi-arid tropics): soil erosion by water and wind, often triggered by human activity.

    Remember it as

    Only ⅓ of cultivated land is irrigated — the rest gambles on the monsoon every single year. Degradation hits irrigated land via salt, rainfed land via erosion.

    01Water Resources of India

    India holds 17%+ of the world's people on just 4% of its water — and only a fraction of that water can actually be used.

    NCERT — Water as a Resource

    Water is a cyclic resource with abundant supplies on the globe. Approximately 71 per cent of the earth's surface is covered with it but freshwater constitutes only about 3 per cent of the total water. In fact, a very small proportion of freshwater is effectively available for human use.

    Key Notes

    • India: 2.45% of world's surface area, 4% of world's water resources, >17% of world's population.
    • Total water available from precipitation annually: ~4,000 cubic km.
    • Available from surface water + replenishable groundwater: 1,869 cubic km — of which only 60% can be put to beneficial use.
    • Total utilisable water resource in the country: only 1,122 cubic km.

    Surface Water Resources

    • Four major sources: rivers, lakes, ponds and tanks — about 10,360 rivers and tributaries longer than 1.6 km each.
    • Mean annual flow in all river basins: 1,869 cubic km — but due to topographical/hydrological constraints, only about 690 cubic km (32%) can be utilised.
    • The Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak basins cover only about ⅓ of the country's area but hold 60% of total surface water resources (high catchment-area rainfall).
    • South Indian rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) have had much of their annual flow already harnessed — unlike the Brahmaputra and Ganga basins.

    Groundwater Resources

    • Total replenishable groundwater: 432 cubic km.
    • High utilisation: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu.
    • Low utilisation: Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Kerala.
    • Moderate utilisation: Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Tripura, Maharashtra.

    Lagoons and Backwaters

    India's indented coastline has formed lagoons and lakes in Kerala, Odisha and West Bengal — water here is generally brackish but used for fishing and irrigating certain paddy varieties, coconut, etc.

    From "available" to "usable" — the water squeeze

    Total precipitation~4,000 km³
    Surface + replenishable groundwater1,869 km³
    Total utilisable water1,122 km³

    Remember it as

    4,000 → 1,869 → 1,122 (all in cubic km): total precipitation → available (surface+groundwater) → actually utilisable. Only 60% of what's "available" can be used.

    02Water Demand and Utilisation

    India's water demand is dominated by one sector above all — irrigation for an agrarian economy.

    NCERT — Sectoral Water Use

    Agriculture accounts for most of the surface and groundwater utilisation — 89 per cent of the surface water and 92 per cent of the groundwater utilisation. The share of the industrial sector is limited to 2 per cent of surface water and 5 per cent of groundwater; the share of the domestic sector is higher (9 per cent) in surface water than in groundwater.

    Table 4.1 — Sectoral Share of Water Utilisation

    SectorSurface WaterGroundwater
    Agriculture89%92%
    Industry2%5%
    Domestic9%3%

    Agriculture dominates both surface and groundwater use; industry and domestic shares are expected to rise as India develops.

    Key Notes — Why irrigation is needed

    • Spatio-temporal variability in rainfall — North-Western India and the Deccan plateau are drought-prone; winter and summer are dry across most of the country.
    • High water-need crops (rice, sugarcane, jute) can only be grown reliably with irrigation.
    • Irrigation enables multiple cropping and higher productivity; HYV crops need regular moisture only irrigation can guarantee.
    • Major multipurpose river valley projects: Bhakra-Nangal, Hirakud, Damodar Valley, Nagarjuna Sagar, Indira Gandhi Canal Project.

    Groundwater over-use — Punjab, Haryana & western UP

    • More than 85% of net sown area is irrigated in Punjab, Haryana and western UP — mainly for wheat and rice.
    • Of net irrigated area, wells/tubewells irrigate 76.1% in Punjab and 51.3% in Haryana — heavy groundwater dependence has caused groundwater table decline.
    • Over-withdrawal has raised fluoride concentration in Rajasthan and Maharashtra, and arsenic concentration in parts of West Bengal and Bihar.

    Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY), 2015-16

    • Har Khet Ko Pani — expand cultivable area under assured irrigation.
    • Integrate water source, distribution and efficient use through appropriate technology.
    • Per Drop More Crop — improve on-farm water-use efficiency, reduce wastage.
    • Introduce sustainable water conservation practices; integrated development of rain-fed areas (watershed approach).

    Remember it as

    Agriculture eats almost all of it: 89% of surface water, 92% of groundwater. Punjab's 76.1% vs Haryana's 51.3% well/tubewell dependence — Punjab is the more groundwater-stressed of the two.

    03Emerging Water Problems

    Falling per-capita availability meets rising pollution — a squeeze from both directions.

    NCERT — Water Quality

    Water quality refers to purity of water, or water without unwanted foreign substances. Water gets polluted by foreign matters such as micro-organisms, chemicals, industrial and other wastes — deteriorating quality and rendering it unfit for human use.

    Key Notes

    • Per-capita water availability is dwindling due to population growth; existing supplies are further degraded by industrial, agricultural and domestic effluents.
    • Rivers retain better quality in less-populated upper (hilly) stretches; in the plains, intensive irrigation/drinking/domestic/industrial use plus drains carrying fertilisers, insecticides, sewage and industrial effluents pollute them.
    • Pollutant concentration in rivers is highest in summer, when water flow is lowest.
    • The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), with State Pollution Control Boards, monitors water quality at 507 stations — organic and bacterial contamination is the main pollution source found.

    Most polluted rivers/stretches (CPCB findings)

    • The Yamuna — the most polluted river in the country, between Delhi and Etawah.
    • Also severely polluted: Sabarmati (Ahmedabad), Gomti (Lucknow), the Kali, the Adyar, the Cooum (entire stretches), the Vaigai (Madurai), the Musi (Hyderabad), and the Ganga at Kanpur and Varanasi.
    • Groundwater pollution: high concentrations of heavy/toxic metals, fluoride and nitrates in different parts of the country.

    Legislation — under-enforced

    • Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Environment Protection Act, 1986 — not implemented effectively.
    • Result: in 1997, 251 polluting industries were located along rivers and lakes.
    • Water Cess Act, 1977 — meant to reduce pollution, but its impact has been only marginal.

    Remember it as

    Most polluted river = Yamuna (Delhi–Etawah). Monitoring: CPCB, 507 stations. Two under-enforced Acts: 1974 (Water) and 1986 (Environment Protection).

    04Water Conservation and Management

    From village percolation tanks to a national policy — India's answer to a resource that's both scarce and shrinking.

    Key Notes — Recycle, Reuse & Watershed Management

    • Recycle and reuse: reclaimed wastewater for industrial cooling/firefighting; household water (after bathing/washing) reused for gardening — conserves better-quality water for drinking.
    • Watershed management: efficient management/conservation of surface and groundwater — prevention of runoff, storage and recharge via percolation tanks, recharge wells; success depends largely on community participation.

    Watershed & conservation programmes

    ProgrammeFocus / Scope
    HaryaliCentral-govt watershed project executed by Gram Panchayats — drinking water, irrigation, fisheries, afforestation.
    Atal Bhujal Yojana (Atal Jal)8,220 water-stressed Gram Panchayats, 229 blocks/talukas, 80 districts, 7 states (Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, MP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, UP) — ~37% of India's water-stressed blocks.
    Neeru-Meeru (Andhra Pradesh)Percolation tanks, dug-out ponds (Johad), check dams via people's participation.
    Arvari Pani Sansad (Alwar, Rajasthan)Same water-harvesting structures, community-led.
    Tamil NaduRainwater harvesting structures made compulsory in every building.

    Case Study — Ralegan Siddhi, Ahmadnagar, Maharashtra

    • 1975: village trapped in poverty and illicit liquor trade; a returning activist convinced villagers of family planning, voluntary labour, and banning open grazing, tree-felling and liquor.
    • Work began with a percolation tank — voluntarily repaired, seven wells below it held water for the first time in living memory.
    • Tarun Mandal (youth group) banned dowry, caste discrimination and untouchability; water-intensive sugarcane was banned, replaced by low-water pulses, oilseeds and cash crops.
    • Nyay Panchayats (informal courts) set up — no case referred to police since. A Rs. 22 lakh school was built using only village resources.
    • Became a national model for watershed-based village transformation.

    Rainwater Harvesting

    • Captures and stores rainwater; recharges groundwater aquifers — low-cost, eco-friendly.
    • Rajasthan's traditional structures: Kund or Tanka — a covered underground tank built near/in the house or village.
    • Benefits: raises water table, dilutes contaminants (fluoride, nitrates), prevents soil erosion and flooding, arrests saltwater intrusion in coastal aquifers, saves pumping energy.

    National Water Policy, 2012 — salient features

    • Push for a national water framework law for optimum development of inter-State rivers and river valleys.
    • Water, after meeting pre-emptive needs (drinking, sanitation, food security, minimum ecosystem needs), to be treated as an economic good.
    • Climate-change adaptation strategies for water infrastructure design/management.
    • Water footprints and water auditing to benchmark efficient use.
    • Remove urban–rural disparity in water-supply norms; manage projects with community participation.

    Jal Kranti Abhiyan (2015-16)

    • One water-stressed village per district (672 districts) developed as a Jal Gram.
    • Model command areas of ~1,000 hectares identified across regions (UP/Haryana–North, Karnataka/Telangana/TN–South, Rajasthan/Gujarat–West, Odisha–East, Meghalaya–North-East).
    • Pollution abatement: conservation + artificial recharge, reducing groundwater pollution, arsenic-free wells.
    • Mass awareness via social media, radio, TV, print, posters, school essay competitions.

    Remember it as

    Kund/Tanka = Rajasthan's underground rainwater tank. Atal Bhujal Yojana = 7 states, 80 districts, 8,220 panchayats. Jal Kranti Abhiyan = 1 Jal Gram per district, 672 districts.

    01Types of Mineral Resources & Their Distribution

    A mineral's fate is decided the moment it forms — whether it carries iron decides which of two great families it belongs to.

    NCERT Definition — Mineral

    A mineral is a natural substance of organic or inorganic origin with definite chemical and physical properties.

    Key Notes — Two Main Categories

    • Metallic minerals — sources of metals (iron ore, copper, gold). Split into Ferrous (iron content — e.g. iron ore) and Non-Ferrous (no iron content — e.g. copper, bauxite).
    • Non-metallic minerals — either organic (fossil/mineral fuels from buried plant/animal life — coal, petroleum) or inorganic (mica, limestone, graphite).

    Three characteristics of minerals

    • Unevenly distributed over space.
    • Inverse relationship between quality and quantity — good-quality minerals are less abundant than low-quality ones.
    • Exhaustible over time — take geological time-scales to form, cannot be replenished on demand, so must be conserved.

    Distribution — Three Mineral Belts of India

    BeltCoverageKey Minerals
    North-Eastern PlateauChhotanagpur (Jharkhand), Odisha Plateau, West Bengal, parts of ChhattisgarhIron ore, coal, manganese, bauxite, mica — most diversified belt
    South-Western PlateauKarnataka, Goa, Tamil Nadu uplands, KeralaFerrous metals, bauxite, high-grade iron ore, manganese, limestone — lacks coal (except Neyveli lignite)
    North-Western RegionAravali (Rajasthan), part of Gujarat — Dharwar system rocksCopper, zinc, building stones (sandstone, granite, marble), gypsum, salt (Rajasthan & Gujarat); Gujarat — petroleum

    A fourth, minor belt — the Himalayan belt — carries copper, lead, zinc, cobalt and tungsten; Assam valley has mineral oil deposits, supplemented by offshore Mumbai High.

    • Over 97% of coal reserves occur in the valleys of the Damodar, Sone, Mahanadi and Godavari.
    • Petroleum reserves: sedimentary basins of Assam, Gujarat and Mumbai High (offshore, Arabian Sea); newer reserves in Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri basins.
    • Most major mineral resources occur east of a line linking Mangaluru and Kanpur.

    Remember it as

    Ferrous = has iron. Non-ferrous = no iron (copper, bauxite). Three belts: NE Plateau (most diverse), SW Plateau (ferrous+bauxite, no coal), NW Region (Aravali — copper/zinc/building stones).

    02Ferrous Minerals — Iron Ore & Manganese

    India's largest reserve of iron ore in Asia sits right next to the coalfields that smelt it — a geological coincidence that built an entire industrial belt.

    NCERT — Ferrous Minerals

    Ferrous minerals such as iron ore, manganese, chromite, etc., provide a strong base for the development of metallurgical industries. India is well-placed in respect of ferrous minerals both in reserves and production.

    Iron Ore

    • India has the largest reserve of iron ore in Asia; two main types — Haematite and Magnetite.
    • About 95% of total iron ore reserves lie in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
    • Iron ore mines occur close to coalfields in the north-eastern plateau region — a major locational advantage.
    • Key mines: Gurumahisani, Sulaipet, Badampahar (Odisha) · Noamundi, Gua (Jharkhand) · Dalli, Rajhara (Chhattisgarh, Durg) · Sandur-Hospet, Kudremukh (Karnataka).

    Manganese

    • Key raw material for smelting iron ore and manufacturing ferro alloys; mainly associated with the Dharwar system.
    • Madhya Pradesh and Odisha are the leading producers; other producers — Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Goa, Jharkhand.
    • Disadvantage: many manganese mines lie far from steel plants.

    Iron ore reserves — top states, visualised

    Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa, Telangana, AP, Tamil Nadu~95%
    All other states combined~5%

    Remember it as

    Iron ore = Haematite + Magnetite, 95% in 8 states led by Odisha/Jharkhand/Chhattisgarh. Manganese = smelts iron + makes ferro-alloys, led by MP and Odisha.

    03Non-Ferrous & Non-Metallic Minerals

    India is metal-poor almost everywhere except one glaring exception — bauxite, the ore aluminium is made from.

    NCERT — Non-Ferrous Minerals

    India is poorly endowed with non-ferrous metallic minerals except bauxite.

    Bauxite

    • Ore used to manufacture aluminium; found in tertiary deposits associated with laterite rocks, on plateaus/hill ranges and coastal tracts.
    • Odisha is the largest producer — Kalahandi and Sambalpur lead, with Bolangir and Koraput rising.
    • Other major producers: Jharkhand (Lohardaga patlands), Gujarat (Bhavnagar, Jamnagar), Chhattisgarh (Amarkantak plateau), Madhya Pradesh (Katni-Jabalpur, Balaghat), Maharashtra (Kolaba, Thane, Ratnagiri, Satara, Pune, Kolhapur).

    Copper

    • Indispensable in the electrical industry (wires, motors, transformers, generators) — alloyable, malleable, ductile; alloyed with gold for jewellery strength.
    • Main deposits: Singhbhum (Jharkhand), Balaghat (MP), Jhunjhunu & Alwar (Rajasthan).
    • Minor producers: Agnigundala (AP), Chitradurg & Hasan (Karnataka), South Arcot (Tamil Nadu).

    Mica (non-metallic)

    • Used in the electrical/electronic industries — splits into thin, tough, flexible sheets.
    • Leading producers: Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Rajasthan — then Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh.
    • Jharkhand's belt: ~150 km long, ~22 km wide in lower Hazaribagh plateau. Rajasthan's belt: ~320 km, Jaipur to Bhilwara/Udaipur. Nellore (AP) produces the best-quality mica.
    • Other non-metallics extracted for local consumption: limestone, dolomite, phosphate.

    Remember it as

    Bauxite → Odisha leads. Copper → Singhbhum (Jharkhand) leads. Mica → Jharkhand's Hazaribagh belt and Rajasthan's Jaipur-Bhilwara belt are the two named belts.

    04Conventional Energy Sources — Coal, Petroleum, Natural Gas & Nuclear

    Four exhaustible sources power almost everything India runs on — and each has its own named heartland.

    Coal

    • Used mainly for thermal power generation and smelting iron ore; occurs in two geological ages — Gondwana and Tertiary deposits.
    • ~80% of India's coal is bituminous, non-coking grade.
    • Most important Gondwana coalfields: Damodar Valley (Jharkhand-Bengal belt) — Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih, Karanpura. Jharia is the largest coalfield, followed by Raniganj.
    • Other coal-bearing valleys: Godavari, Mahanadi, Sone. Key mining centres: Singrauli (MP/UP), Korba (Chhattisgarh), Talcher (Odisha), Chanda-Wardha (Maharashtra), Singareni (Telangana).
    • Tertiary coals: Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Nagaland. Lignite (brown coal): Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Gujarat, J&K.

    Petroleum

    • Called "liquid gold" for its scarcity and diverse uses; occurs in sedimentary rocks of the Tertiary period.
    • ONGC (Oil and Natural Gas Commission) set up in 1956 — before that, Digboi (Assam) was India's only oil-producing region.
    • Key oilfields: Digboi, Naharkatiya, Moran (Assam) · Ankaleshwar, Kalol, Mehsana, Nawagam (Gujarat) · Mumbai High (160 km offshore, discovered 1973, production from 1976) · Krishna-Godavari & Kaveri basins (east coast).
    • Two refinery types: field-based (e.g. Digboi) and market-based (e.g. Barauni).

    Natural Gas & Nuclear Energy

    • Natural gas is found with petroleum; major reserves — Mumbai High and west coast fields (supplemented by Cambay basin), plus new Krishna-Godavari basin finds on the east coast. Used as CNG (transport) and PNG (cooking).
    • Uranium: Singhbhum copper belt, plus Udaipur/Alwar/Jhunjhunu (Rajasthan), Durg (Chhattisgarh), Bhandara (Maharashtra), Kullu (HP).
    • Thorium: from monazite/ilmenite beach sands of Kerala & Tamil Nadu — world's richest monazite deposits in Palakkad & Kollam (Kerala), near Vishakhapatnam (AP), Mahanadi delta (Odisha).
    • Atomic Energy Commission: 1948. Atomic Energy Institute, Trombay (1954) → renamed Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, 1967.
    • Nuclear power projects: Tarapur (Maharashtra, India's first), Rawatbhata (Rajasthan), Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu), Narora (UP), Kaiga (Karnataka), Kakarapara (Gujarat).

    Remember it as

    Jharia = largest coalfield. Mumbai High = discovered 1973, produced from 1976. ONGC = 1956. Bhabha Atomic Research Centre = renamed 1967 (est. as Trombay Institute, 1954). Tarapur = India's first nuclear power station.

    05Non-Conventional Energy Sources & Conservation

    Solar, wind, tidal, geothermal and bio-energy — renewable, equitable and the direction India's energy mix is heading.

    NCERT — Why Non-Conventional?

    Sustainable energy resources are only the renewable energy sources — solar, wind, hydro-geothermal and biomass. These are more equitably distributed and environment-friendly, and provide more sustained, eco-friendly, cheaper energy after the initial cost is met.

    Five renewable sources

    SourceKey Facts
    SolarPhotovoltaics + solar thermal technology; 7% more effective than coal/oil plants, 10% more than nuclear plants; greatest potential in Gujarat & Rajasthan.
    WindPollution-free, inexhaustible; kinetic energy of wind → electrical energy via turbines; favourable conditions in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka.
    Tidal & WaveLarge tidal waves occur along India's west coast — great potential, but not yet utilised.
    GeothermalHeat from magma / hot geyser water converted to electrical energy; India's plant commissioned at Manikaran, Himachal Pradesh.
    Bio-energyFrom agricultural residues, municipal/industrial waste — converts to electricity, heat or cooking gas; example project: Okhla, Delhi (municipal waste to energy).

    Conservation of Mineral Resources

    • Sustainable development needs resource protection for future generations — traditional use generates waste and environmental problems.
    • Replace exhaustible resources with inexhaustible alternatives (solar, wind, wave, geothermal).
    • Recycling scrap metal is especially significant for copper, lead and zinc — metals where India's own reserves are meagre.
    • Use of substitutes for scarce metals; reduce export of strategic and scarce minerals to extend the life of existing reserves.

    Solar effectiveness vs conventional plants

    Solar vs Coal/Oil plants+7% more effective
    Solar vs Nuclear plants+10% more effective

    Remember it as

    Solar/Wind = Gujarat & Rajasthan's strength. Geothermal = Manikaran (HP). Bio-energy waste-to-power = Okhla (Delhi). Conserve scarce metals (copper, lead, zinc) via scrap recycling and reduced exports.

    01Planning Approaches — Sectoral, Regional & NITI Aayog

    Planning stopped being a hit-and-miss method the day it became a deliberate process of thinking, formulating and implementing a scheme to reach a goal.

    NCERT — Two Approaches to Planning

    Sectoral planning means formulation and implementation of schemes aimed at development of various sectors of the economy — agriculture, irrigation, manufacturing, power, transport, communication, social infrastructure and services. Regional planning takes a spatial perspective to reduce regional imbalance, since economic development is never uniform over space.

    Target Area & Target Group Approaches

    • Even resource-rich regions can remain backward — development needs technology and investment, not just resources.
    • After ~1.5 decades of planning experience, regional imbalances were seen to be worsening, so the Planning Commission introduced 'target area' and 'target group' approaches.
    • Target area programmes: Command Area Development Programme, Drought Prone Area Programme, Desert Development Programme, Hill Area Development Programme.
    • Target group programmes: Small Farmers Development Agency (SFDA), Marginal Farmers Development Agency (MFDA).
    • 8th Five Year Plan: special area programmes for hill areas, north-eastern states, tribal areas, backward areas.

    NITI Aayog

    • India adopted centralised planning after Independence, later moving to decentralised multi-level planning (Centre, State, district).
    • On 1 January 2015, the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog.
    • Objective: involve states in economic policy-making, providing strategic and technical advice to Central and State governments.

    Remember it as

    Sectoral = by SECTOR (agriculture, power...). Regional = by SPACE (reduce imbalance). NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.

    02Drought Prone Area Programme & Hill Area Development Programme

    Two of India's earliest target-area programmes — one for the driest tracts, one for the highest ones.

    Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP)

    • Initiated during the Fourth Five Year Plan — originally to provide employment and create productive assets via labour-intensive civil works; later shifted to irrigation projects, land development, afforestation, grassland development and rural infrastructure.
    • Planning Commission (1967) identified 67 districts prone to drought. Irrigation Commission (1972) introduced the criterion of 30% irrigated area to demarcate drought-prone areas.
    • Spreads over semi-arid/arid Rajasthan, Gujarat, western MP, Marathwada (Maharashtra), Rayalseema & Telangana plateaus (AP), Karnataka plateau, interior Tamil Nadu.
    • Punjab, Haryana and north-Rajasthan are largely protected due to spread of irrigation.
    • Strategy needed: integrated watershed development at the micro-level, restoring balance between water, soil, plants, humans and animals.

    Hill Area Development Programme

    • Initiated during the Fifth Five Year Plan, covering 15 districts — all hilly districts of UP (now Uttarakhand), Mikir Hill & North Cachar hills (Assam), Darjeeling (West Bengal), Nilgiri (Tamil Nadu).
    • National Committee on Development of Backward Areas (1981) recommended treating all hill areas above 600 m (not under tribal sub-plan) as backward hill areas.
    • Focus: horticulture, plantation, agriculture, animal husbandry, poultry, forestry, small-scale/village industry — plans drawn around topographical, ecological, social and economic conditions.

    Remember it as

    DPAP = Fourth Plan, 67 districts (1967), 30% irrigation criterion (1972). Hill Area Development = Fifth Plan, 15 districts, >600m altitude rule (1981).

    03Case Study — Integrated Tribal Development Project, Bharmaur

    A remote Himalayan homeland of the Gaddi tribe, transformed by half a century of targeted planning — but unevenly, village by village.

    NCERT — Bharmaur Tribal Region

    Bharmaur is inhabited by 'Gaddi', a tribal community who have maintained a distinct identity in the Himalayan region as they practised transhumance and conversed through the Gaddiali dialect.
    • Bharmaur tribal area = Bharmaur + Holi tehsils, Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh — notified tribal area since 21 November 1975.
    • 2011 Census: population 39,113, density 21 persons/sq km — one of the most backward areas (economically & socially) of HP.
    • Area ~1,818 sq km, between 1,500–3,700 m altitude; bounded by Pir Panjal (north) and Dhaula Dhar (south), converging near Rohtang Pass.
    • Drained by the river Ravi and tributaries the Budhil and Tundahen, dividing the region into four physiographic divisions: Holi, Khani, Kugti and Tundah.
    • Mean monthly temperature: 4°C in January, 26°C in July.

    Development timeline & social benefits

    • 1970s: Gaddis included among Scheduled Tribes. 1974: tribal sub-plan introduced under the Fifth Five Year Plan; Bharmaur designated one of 5 ITDPs (Integrated Tribal Development Projects) in Himachal Pradesh.
    • Plan priorities: transport & communications, agriculture & allied activities, social & community services.
    • Infrastructure gains concentrated along the river Ravi in Holi and Khani — remote Tundah and Kugti areas still under-served.
    • Female literacy rose from 1.88% (1971) to 65% (2011) — gender inequality in literacy also declined; sex ratio improved; child marriage declined.
    • Traditional subsistence agro-pastoral economy is shifting — pulses/cash crops rising, but only ~1/10th of households still practise transhumance; many Gaddis migrate seasonally to Kangra for wage labour.

    Remember it as

    Bharmaur = Gaddi tribe, Chamba (HP), ITDP since 1974. Female literacy: 1.88% → 65% (1971→2011). Four divisions: Holi, Khani, Kugti, Tundah.

    04Sustainable Development

    Development stopped meaning just GNP growth once the world noticed that growth alone could still leave people poorer — and the planet worse off.

    NCERT — The Brundtland Definition (1987)

    The World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED), headed by Norwegian PM Gro Harlem Brundtland, gave its report ('Our Common Future', 1987) defining sustainable development as "development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs."

    How the idea of "development" evolved

    • Post-WWII era: development = economic growth, measured by rising GNP and per-capita income/consumption.
    • High-growth countries still saw rising poverty due to unequal distribution — so in the 1970s, "redistribution with growth" and "growth and equity" entered the definition.
    • By the 1980s: development broadened to include health, education, equality of opportunity, and political/civil rights — widespread social AND material well-being.

    Roots of the sustainability idea

    • Emerged from rising environmental awareness in the late 1960s in the Western world, reacting to industrial development's undesirable environmental effects.
    • Key publications that raised alarm: 'The Population Bomb' (Ehrlich, 1968) and 'The Limits to Growth' (Meadows and others, 1972).
    • Sustainable development balances ecological, social and economic aspects — conserving resources so future generations can also use them; it is about the common future of all humankind.

    Remember it as

    Brundtland Report = 'Our Common Future', 1987 — the exact definition is CUET gold. Timeline: Population Bomb (1968) → Limits to Growth (1972) → Brundtland Report (1987).

    05Case Study — Indira Gandhi Canal Command Area

    A desert transformed into farmland — and a textbook example of how irrigation success can create its own environmental problems.

    NCERT — Indira Gandhi Canal

    Previously known as the Rajasthan Canal, conceived by Kanwar Sain in 1948, the project was launched on 31 March 1958. It originates at the Harike barrage in Punjab and runs parallel to the Pakistan border through the Thar Desert (Marusthali) of Rajasthan.
    • Total planned length: 9,060 km, culturable command area: 19.63 lakh hectares — ~70% by flow system, rest by lift system.
    • Stage-I: Ganganagar, Hanumangarh, northern Bikaner — 5.53 lakh ha, gently undulating; irrigation began early 1960s.
    • Stage-II: Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur, Churu — 14.10 lakh ha, shifting sand dunes, up to 50°C summers; irrigation began mid-1980s.
    • All lift canals originate from the left bank of the main canal; all flow channels are on the right bank.

    Impact — both ways

    • Positive: greened the desert; reduced wind erosion and canal siltation; traditional crops (gram, bajra, jowar) replaced by wheat, cotton, groundnut, rice; big rise in agricultural & livestock productivity.
    • Negative: intensive irrigation + excessive water use → twin problems of waterlogging and soil salinity, threatening long-run agricultural sustainability.

    Seven Measures for Sustainable Development

    Five of the seven are meant specifically to restore ecological balance.

    1. Strict implementation of water management policy — protective irrigation in Stage-I, extensive irrigation + pasture development in Stage-II.
    2. Avoid water-intensive crops in the cropping pattern; encourage plantation crops like citrus fruits.
    3. Effective CAD programmes — lining of water courses, land development/levelling, warabandi (equal distribution of canal water) — to cut conveyance loss.
    4. Reclaim areas affected by waterlogging and soil salinity.
    5. Eco-development — afforestation, shelterbelt plantation, pasture development, especially in fragile Stage-II.
    6. Social sustainability — financial/institutional support for poor land allottees.
    7. Economic sustainability — diversify beyond agriculture/animal husbandry; build links between villages, agro-service centres and market centres.

    Remember it as

    Kanwar Sain conceived it in 1948, launched 1958. Stage-I (1960s) vs Stage-II (1980s). Twin problems: waterlogging + soil salinity. 5 of 7 sustainability measures target ECOLOGICAL balance.

    01Road Transport

    India's roads carry the overwhelming majority of both passengers and freight — and just 2% of that network (the National Highways) carries 40% of all road traffic.

    NCERT — Road Transport in India

    India has one of the largest road networks in the world, with a total length of about 62.16 lakh km. About 85% of passenger and 70% of freight traffic is carried by roads every year.

    Table 7.1 — India's Road Network, 2020

    Road CategoryLength (km)
    National Highways1,36,440
    State Highways1,76,818
    Other Roads59,02,539
    Total62,15,797

    Key Notes

    • National Highways (NH): built/maintained by the Centre; inter-state, defence and strategic connectivity. Grew from 19,700 km (1951) to 1,36,440 km (2020) — only ~2% of total road length but carries 40% of road traffic.
    • NHAI (National Highways Authority of India) operationalised in 1995 — develops, maintains and operates National Highways.
    • State Highways: built/maintained by states — link state capitals with district HQs and connect to NHs.
    • Rural Roads: ~80% of India's total road length — density varies with terrain.
    • Other Roads: Border Roads (Border Roads Organisation, est. May 1960) and International Highways.

    Landmark Road Projects

    • Golden Quadrilateral: 5,846 km, 4/6-lane corridor connecting Delhi-Mumbai-Chennai-Kolkata.
    • North-South Corridor: 4,076 km, Srinagar to Kanniyakumari (incl. Cochin-Salem spur). East-West Corridor: 3,640 km, Silchar to Porbandar.
    • Bharatmala Pariyojana: ~26,000 km of Economic Corridors, plus ring roads/bypasses/elevated corridors to decongest cities.
    • Atal Tunnel (9.02 km) — world's longest highway tunnel, built by BRO, connects Manali to Lahaul-Spiti year-round, at 3,000m in the Pir Panjal range.
    • Grand Trunk Road: originally the Shahi (Royal) Road built by Sher Shah Suri from Indus Valley to Sonar Valley (Bengal); renamed GT Road under British rule; today runs Amritsar to Kolkata.

    Road network composition, visualised

    Other Roads~95%
    State Highways~2.8%
    National Highways~2.2%

    National Highways are only ~2% of total road length by distance — but carry 40% of all road traffic.

    Remember it as

    NH = 2% of length, 40% of traffic. NHAI = 1995. Golden Quadrilateral = 5,846 km. Atal Tunnel = 9.02 km, world's longest highway tunnel.

    02Rail Transport

    India's railway system began with a 34 km line in 1853 — today it is one of the longest networks on earth, run through 17 zones.

    NCERT — Indian Railways

    Indian Railways was introduced in 1853, when a line was constructed from Bombay to Thane covering a distance of 34 km. It is the largest government undertaking in the country, with a network length of 67,956 km (2019-20).

    Three Gauges

    GaugeTrack WidthLength (2019-20)
    Broad Gauge1.676 m63,950 km
    Metre Gauge1 m2,402 km
    Narrow Gauge0.762 m or 0.610 m1,604 km (mainly hilly areas)

    Key Notes

    • India's railway system is divided into 17 zones for management — e.g. Northern (New Delhi), Southern (Chennai), Central (Mumbai CST), Metro Railway (Kolkata).
    • Steam engines have been replaced by diesel and electric — raising speed, haulage capacity and reducing station pollution.
    • Railway network is relatively less dense in hill states, north-eastern states, central India and Rajasthan.
    • Konkan Railway (1998): 760 km, Roha (Maharashtra) to Mangaluru (Karnataka) — crosses 146 rivers/streams, ~2,000 bridges, 91 tunnels, including Asia's largest tunnel (~6.5 km); joint undertaking of Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka.
    • Metro rail has revolutionised urban transport; CNG buses + metro help control urban air pollution.

    Remember it as

    1853 = Bombay–Thane, 34 km, India's first railway. 17 zones. Broad gauge = 1.676m (largest share). Konkan Railway = 1998, 760 km, Roha–Mangaluru.

    03Water & Air Transport, and Pipelines

    The cheapest way to move heavy cargo and the fastest way to move people and perishables — at opposite ends of India's transport spectrum.

    Water Transport

    • Two types: Inland waterways and Oceanic routes. Cheapest, most fuel-efficient, eco-friendly mode — best for heavy, bulky cargo.
    • India has 14,500 km of navigable waterways, contributing ~1% of the country's transportation.
    • 111 inland waterways (including 5 earlier National Waterways) declared National Waterways under the National Waterways Act, 2016; managed by the Inland Waterways Authority (est. 1986).
    • NW-1 (Prayagraj-Haldia, 1,620 km, on the Ganga) is India's most important waterway. NW-2 runs on the Brahmaputra (Sadiya-Dhubri). NW-3 uses the West Coast Canal (Kottapuram-Kollam, Kerala).
    • Oceanic routes: India's coastline is ~7,517 km; 12 major and 200 minor ports; ~95% of India's foreign trade by volume (~70% by value) moves via ocean routes.

    Air Transport

    • Fastest mode — began in 1911 with airmail over 10 km (Prayagraj to Naini); real growth came post-Independence.
    • Airport Authority of India ensures safe, efficient air traffic and aeronautical communication.
    • UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik) — Regional Connectivity Scheme by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, making flying affordable and boosting regional/remote air connectivity; 73 unserved/underserved airports (incl. 9 heliports, 2 water aerodromes) operationalised since 2017.
    • Pawan Hans — helicopter service, mainly in hilly north-eastern areas, and for petroleum-sector/tourism transport.

    Oil & Gas Pipelines

    • Most convenient/efficient way to transport liquids and gases over long distances; even solids can move via pipeline as slurry.
    • Oil India Limited (OIL), incorporated 1959, built Asia's first cross-country pipeline: 1,157 km, Naharkatiya (Assam) to Barauni (Bihar), later extended to Kanpur (1966).
    • GAIL (India) Ltd. set up in 1984; built the Hazira-Vijaipur-Jagdishpur (HVJ) pipeline — 1,700 km — linking Mumbai High/Bassein gas fields to fertiliser/power/industrial complexes.
    • India's gas pipeline network has expanded from 1,700 km to 18,500 km, expected to reach over 34,000 km as a national Gas Grid.

    Remember it as

    Water: 14,500 km navigable, 111 National Waterways (2016 Act). Air: UDAN + Pawan Hans. Pipelines: OIL (1959, Naharkatiya-Barauni) and GAIL (1984, HVJ pipeline).

    04Communication Networks

    From drumbeats and smoke signals to satellites — communication has always run alongside transport, just at a different speed.

    NCERT — Modes of Communication

    On the basis of scale and quality, modes of communication are divided into Personal Communication System and Mass Communication System.

    Personal & Mass Communication

    • Personal Communication: the internet is the most effective/advanced — enables direct e-mail contact, e-commerce, and low-cost access to information.
    • Radio: began 1923 (Radio Club of Bombay); brought under government control 1930 as the Indian Broadcasting System; renamed All India Radio (1936), then Akashwani (1957).
    • Television: began in Delhi (1959), expanded to other centres after 1972; delinked from AIR in 1976, becoming Doordarshan (DD). Common National Programmes started after INSAT-1A.

    Satellite Communication

    • Two systems: INSAT (Indian National Satellite System, established 1983 — telecommunication, meteorology, other data) and IRS (Indian Remote Sensing Satellite System — began with IRS-1A, March 1988, launched from Baikonur, Russia).
    • India developed its own launch vehicle: PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle).
    • National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad — acquires and processes satellite data, vital for natural resource management.
    • Satellite images are used for weather forecasting, monitoring natural calamities, and border surveillance.

    Remember it as

    Radio: 1923 → 1936 (AIR) → 1957 (Akashwani). TV: 1959 (Delhi) → 1976 delinked as Doordarshan. INSAT = 1983. IRS-1A = March 1988.

    01Changing Pattern of India's Foreign Trade

    India's trade grew over 6,000-fold in seventy years — but imports have almost always outrun exports.

    NCERT — India's Trade Growth

    In 1950-51, India's external trade was worth Rs. 1,214 crore, which rose to Rs. 77,19,796 crore in 2020-21. India's contribution to world trade is as low as 1% of the total volume, yet it plays a significant role in the world economy.

    Table 8.1 — India's Foreign Trade (Rs. Crore)

    YearExportsImportsTrade Balance
    2004-053,75,3405,01,065−1,25,725
    2009-108,45,53413,63,736−5,18,202
    2013-1419,05,01127,15,434−8,10,423
    2016-1718,52,34025,77,422−7,25,082
    2021-2231,47,02145,72,775−14,25,753

    India's trade balance has been persistently negative — imports have consistently exceeded exports.

    Composition of Exports (% share)

    Commodity2015-162021-22
    Agriculture & allied products12.6%11.9%
    Ore and minerals1.6%2.0%
    Manufactured goods72.9%67.8%
    Crude and petroleum products11.9%16.4%
    • Manufacturing alone = 67.8% of export value (2021-22); share of agriculture & manufactured goods has DECLINED, while crude petroleum & other commodities have RISEN.
    • Traditional export items (e.g. cashew) are declining due to tough international competition; floriculture, fresh fruits, marine products and sugar are rising.

    Composition of Imports (% share)

    • 1950s-60s: food shortage → major imports were foodgrain, capital goods, machinery. After 1970s, foodgrain imports discontinued (Green Revolution success).
    • 1973 energy crisis pushed petroleum prices up — foodgrain import replaced by fertiliser and petroleum imports.
    • Fuel (coal, POL) rose from 25.4% (2015-16) to 31.6% (2021-22) — the single largest and fastest-rising import category; capital goods import share has steadily declined.

    Remember it as

    1950-51: Rs. 1,214 crore → 2020-21: Rs. 77,19,796 crore. India = only 1% of world trade volume. Manufacturing = 67.8% of exports; Fuel = 31.6% of imports (2021-22), both the single largest category in their column.

    02Direction of Trade

    India trades with the whole world — but Asia and ASEAN alone account for the largest single share.

    NCERT — Direction of Trade

    India has trade relations with most countries and major trading blocks of the world. Most of India's foreign trade is carried through sea and air routes; a small portion moves by land to neighbouring Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

    Table 8.6 — Direction of India's Import Trade (Rs. Crore)

    Region2016-172021-22
    Europe4,03,9726,40,577
    Africa1,93,3273,68,156
    North America1,95,3323,78,041
    Latin America1,15,7621,61,995
    Asia and ASEAN15,44,52029,18,577

    Asia and ASEAN is by far India's largest import-origin region — nearly double Europe, its nearest rival.

    • India aims to double its share in international trade within five years, via import liberalisation, lower import duties, delicensing, and a shift from process to product patents.
    • China and other East Asian countries are India's major export competitors.

    Asia/ASEAN's dominance, visualised

    Asia and ASEAN₹29,18,577 cr
    Europe₹6,40,577 cr
    North America₹3,78,041 cr
    Africa₹3,68,156 cr

    Remember it as

    Asia+ASEAN = India's biggest import source (2021-22: ₹29.19 lakh crore) — bigger than Europe, N.America and Africa combined. Trade mostly moves by sea and air; only land-route trade goes to Nepal/Bhutan/Bangladesh/Pakistan.

    03Sea Ports as Gateways of International Trade

    Twelve major ports and 200 minor ones turn India's 7,500+ km coastline into its busiest trade corridor — carrying 95% of trade by volume.

    NCERT — Ports

    India has 12 major ports and 200 minor/intermediate ports. The Central Government decides policy for major ports; state governments regulate minor ports. Major ports handle the larger share of total traffic.

    India's 12 Major Ports

    PortKey Facts
    Deendayal (Kandla)Gulf of Kuchchh — serves NW India; petroleum/fertiliser focus; offshore terminal at Vadinar.
    MumbaiIndia's biggest natural harbour, largest oil terminal; hinterland — MP, Maharashtra, Gujarat, UP, Rajasthan.
    Jawaharlal Nehru (Nhava Sheva)Satellite port to Mumbai; India's largest container port.
    MormugaoGoa, natural harbour; remodelled 1961 for iron-ore export to Japan; hinterland extended by Konkan Railway.
    New MangaloreKarnataka; iron-ore/concentrate exports, fertilisers, petroleum.
    Cochin'Queen of the Arabian Sea', natural harbour near Suez-Colombo route; serves Kerala/S.Karnataka/SW Tamil Nadu.
    Shyama Prasad Mookerjee (Kolkata)On the Hugli, 128 km inland; silt-accumulation problem; extends to Nepal/Bhutan.
    Haldia105 km downstream of Kolkata — relieves Kolkata's congestion; bulk cargo (iron ore, coal, petroleum).
    ParadwipMahanadi delta; deepest harbour, large-scale iron-ore export; hinterland Odisha/Chhattisgarh/Jharkhand.
    VisakhapatnamLand-locked harbour, channel cut through rock; iron-ore, petroleum, general cargo.
    ChennaiOldest artificial harbour (built 1859) on east coast; not suited to large ships (shallow water).
    Kamarajar (Ennore) & V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin)Both relieve pressure on Chennai port.
    • India's west coast has more ports than the east coast — many carry the suffix "pattan" (port) in their names.
    • Partition cost India two major ports: Karachi (to Pakistan) and Chittagong (to East Pakistan/Bangladesh) — compensated by developing Kandla and Diamond Harbour.
    • Port capacity rose from 20 million tonnes (1951) to over 837 million tonnes (2016).

    Remember it as

    12 major + 200 minor ports. West coast has MORE ports than east. JNPT = largest container port. Vizag = land-locked harbour. Partition cost India Karachi and Chittagong.

    04Airports in International Trade

    The fastest, costliest route for India's trade — built for speed and high-value cargo, not bulk.

    NCERT — Air Transport in Trade

    Air transport has the advantage of taking the least time for carriage and handling high-value or perishable goods over long distances. It is very costly and unsuitable for carrying heavy and bulky commodities — reducing its share in international trade compared to oceanic routes.
    • 25 major airports were functioning in the country as per the Annual Report 2016-17 — including Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Delhi, Goa, Guwahati, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai, Thiruvananthapuram, Srinagar and more.
    • Since 2017, under the UDAN scheme, a total of 73 unserved/underserved airports — including 9 heliports and 2 water aerodromes — have been operationalised.

    Sea vs Air — the trade-off

    ModeAdvantageDisadvantage
    Sea (oceanic routes)Handles ~95% of trade BY VOLUME — cheap for bulky/heavy cargoSlow
    AirFastest; ideal for high-value/perishable goodsVery costly; unsuitable for bulky cargo

    Remember it as

    Air = fastest + costliest, best for high-value/perishable goods. 25 major airports (2016-17). UDAN (since 2017) = 73 unserved/underserved airports operationalised, incl. 9 heliports + 2 water aerodromes.

    01Environmental Pollution

    Air, water, land and noise pollution are four faces of the same problem — waste and energy released from human activity, faster than nature can absorb it.

    NCERT — Environmental Pollution

    Environmental pollution results from "the release of substances and energy from waste products of human activities." Pollution is classified into (i) air pollution, (ii) water pollution, (iii) land pollution, and (iv) noise pollution.

    Table 9.1 — Types and Sources of Pollution

    TypeKey PollutantsMain Sources
    AirOxides of sulphur/nitrogen, CO, hydrocarbons, leadCombustion of coal/petrol/diesel, industry, waste/sewage disposal
    WaterAmmonia, nitrates, heavy metals (lead, arsenic, mercury), pesticide residueSewage, urban run-off, toxic industrial effluents, nuclear plants
    LandExcreta, pathogens, pesticide/fertiliser residueImproper waste disposal, pesticide/fertiliser overuse
    NoiseSound above tolerance levelAircraft, automobiles, trains, industry, advertising

    Water Pollution

    • Industry is the most significant polluter — chief water-polluting industries: leather, pulp & paper, textiles, chemicals.
    • The WHO estimates about one-fourth of India's communicable diseases are water-borne (diarrhoea, intestinal worms, hepatitis, etc.).
    • Ganga pollution — worst downstream of Kanpur, downstream of Varanasi, and at the Farakka Barrage; polluters include Kanpur's industries and urban domestic waste from Kanpur, Prayagraj, Varanasi, Patna, Kolkata.
    • Yamuna pollution — Delhi to confluence with Chambal, and at Mathura/Agra; caused by Haryana/UP irrigation extraction, agricultural run-off, and Delhi's domestic + industrial waste.

    Namami Gange Programme

    • Union Government scheme to clean the Ganga: sewerage treatment in towns, monitoring industrial effluents, river-front development, afforestation along banks, cleaning the river surface, developing 'Ganga Grams' (Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal), and public awareness.

    Air & Noise Pollution

    • Air pollution: addition of contaminants (dust, fumes, gas, smoke) to the air, harmful to flora/fauna/property; chiefly from fossil fuel combustion, mining and industry. Causes "urban smog" and can cause acid rain — the first rain after summer has a lower pH than subsequent rains.
    • Noise pollution: unbearable/uncomfortable noise; biggest source is traffic (aircraft, automobiles, trains); intensity declines with distance from source.

    Case Study — Daurala, Meerut (Restoring Ecology & Health)

    • Based on the "Polluter Pays" principle — untreated wastewater from Daurala industries had contaminated groundwater with heavy metals.
    • A Meerut-based NGO's door-to-door health survey (2003) drove reforms: expanded water tank capacity, 900m extra pipeline for potable water, desilted village pond, rainwater harvesting structures, and 1,000 trees planted.

    Remember it as

    4 types of pollution: air, water, land, noise. Ganga's worst stretches: Kanpur, Varanasi, Farakka. Yamuna's worst stretch: Delhi–Chambal confluence. Daurala = "Polluter Pays" case study.

    02Urban Waste Disposal

    India's metros collect nearly all their waste — its smaller towns collect barely half.

    NCERT — Solid Waste

    Solid waste refers to a variety of old and used articles — stained metal pieces, broken glassware, plastic containers, polythene bags, ash, etc. — disposed of from two sources: (i) household/domestic establishments, and (ii) industrial/commercial establishments.

    Key Notes

    • In metros like Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru — about 90% of solid waste is collected and disposed.
    • In most OTHER cities/towns, 30-50% of waste generated is left uncollected — accumulating on streets, open spaces and wastelands.
    • Uncollected waste causes health hazards — obnoxious smell, and harbours flies/rodents that spread typhoid, diphtheria, diarrhoea, malaria, cholera.
    • Untreated waste ferments slowly and releases toxic biogas (including methane) into the atmosphere; wastes should instead be treated as a resource — for energy and compost.
    • The Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) — part of India's urban renewal mission, aims to improve quality of life in urban slums.

    Waste collection — metros vs other towns

    Metros (Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru)~90% collected
    Most other cities/towns50–70% collected

    30–50% of waste in most non-metro towns is left UNCOLLECTED — the mirror image of the "collected" figure.

    Remember it as

    Metros collect ~90% of waste; other towns leave 30–50% uncollected. Untreated waste → toxic biogas (methane). Waste = a resource, not just a problem.

    03Rural–Urban Migration

    Push factors at home and pull factors in the city drive one of India's most consistent population movements — dominated, and defined, by men leaving alone.

    NCERT — Why People Migrate

    Population flow from rural to urban areas is caused by high demand for labour in urban areas, low job opportunities in rural areas, and unbalanced development between urban and rural areas. Poor migrants often bypass small/medium cities to go directly to mega cities for livelihood.

    Case Study — Ramesh (Welder, Odisha to Gujarat/Maharashtra)

    • Worked on contract in Talcher (Odisha coal region), then moved with his contractor across Surat, Mumbai, Gandhinagar, Bharuch, Jamnagar.
    • Remits ~Rs. 20,000/year to his family — used for consumption, healthcare, schooling, and some agriculture/land/house investment.
    • Originally forced to migrate by poverty (family survived on 3 acres, high debt); first went to Ludhiana in 1988 at Rs. 20/day wages, then moved to Surat to learn welding.
    • Family's standard of living improved significantly, but Ramesh bears the pain of separation — his job's temporary, transferable nature prevents relocating his family with him.
    • In developing countries, poor/semi-illiterate/unskilled migrants like Ramesh typically end up in menial, low-wage, informal-sector urban jobs.
    • Since urban wages are too low to support a whole family, spouses/children/elderly are often left behind in rural areas — so the rural-urban migration stream is dominated by males.

    Remember it as

    Push (rural poverty/low jobs) + Pull (urban labour demand) = migration. Ramesh's case: male-dominated migration stream — low urban wages force families to stay behind.

    04Problems of Slums

    Where the poorest migrants land when they can't afford proper housing — overcrowded, under-served, and often the very engine of the city's wealth.

    NCERT — Slums

    Slums are residential areas of the least choice — dilapidated houses, poor hygienic conditions, poor ventilation, lack of basic amenities like drinking water, light and toilet facilities. Open defecation, unregulated drainage and overcrowded narrow streets are serious health and socio-environmental hazards.

    Key Notes

    • India remains predominantly rural — approx. 69% rural population (2011); urban centres are far more differentiated (socio-economic, politico-cultural) than rural areas.
    • At one extreme: farm houses and high-income localities with wide roads, streetlights, water/sanitation, parks. At the other: slums and jhuggi-jhopari clusters, inhabited by those who migrated for livelihood but couldn't afford proper housing due to high rent/land cost.
    • Most slum residents work in low-paid, high-risk, unorganised urban jobs — leading to undernourishment, disease, poor education access, and vulnerability to drug abuse, crime and social exclusion.
    • The Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) is part of the urban renewal mission aimed at improving urban slum quality of life.

    Case Study — Dharavi, Asia's Largest Slum (Mumbai)

    • Formed on land reclaimed from the sea, largely by Scheduled Castes and poor Muslim migrants.
    • Extreme overcrowding — narrow lanes too small even for a bicycle; buildings 2-3 storeys, a single room often housing 12+ people.
    • Yet Dharavi produces high-value goods — ceramics, embroidery, zari work, leather goods, high-fashion garments, jewellery settings, wood carvings — feeding the wealth of the city that shuns it (Seabrook, 1996).

    Remember it as

    Dharavi = Asia's LARGEST slum, Mumbai — reclaimed sea-land, home to high-value craft industries despite dire conditions. Slum growth = migration + unaffordable formal housing.

    05Land Degradation

    Land doesn't disappear when it's overused — it just stops producing, and the damage can be natural, human-made, or both.

    NCERT — Land Degradation

    Land degradation is generally understood as either a temporary or permanent decline in the productive capacity of land. Soil erosion, waterlogging, salinisation and alkalinisation lead to land degradation; unchecked degradation may convert land to wasteland.

    Key Notes — Two Causes, Three Categories

    • Natural causes only: gullied/ravinous land, desertic/coastal sands, barren rocky areas, steep sloping land, glacial areas.
    • Natural + human causes: waterlogged/marshy areas, land affected by salinity/alkalinity, land with/without scrub.
    • Human-made causes (primarily): degraded shifting-cultivation area, degraded plantation-crop land, degraded forests, degraded pastures, mining/industrial wastelands.
    • The National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) classifies wastelands using remote sensing — man-made degradation processes are found to be MORE significant than natural ones.

    Case Study — Jhabua District, Madhya Pradesh

    • Westernmost agro-climatic zone of MP; one of India's five most backward districts; high concentration of tribal population (mostly Bhils).
    • Poverty accentuated by severe forest and land degradation; Watershed Management Programmes (funded by Ministries of Rural Development and Agriculture) treated 20% of the district's area in five years.
    • Petlawad block (Sat Rundi hamlet, Karravat village) — a successful Government-NGO-community partnership: households planted/maintained trees on Common Property Resources, planted fodder grass, adopted "social fencing" (no open grazing, stall-feeding instead).
    • An encroachment dispute over common land was resolved by making the encroacher a member of the user group — sharing benefits of greened common land instead of litigation.

    Remember it as

    3 categories: natural-only, natural+human, human-made(mostly). NRSC = classifies wastelands. Jhabua = Bhils, Petlawad block, watershed management + social fencing success story.

    01Nature of Human Geography

    Nature and human beings are so intricately intertwined that even our language borrows the human body to describe the earth — the 'face' of the earth, the 'mouth' of a river.

    Human Geography — Three Classic Definitions

    Ratzel: "Human geography is the synthetic study of relationship between human societies and earth's surface."
    Ellen C. Semple: "Human geography is the study of the changing relationship between the unresting man and the unstable earth."
    Paul Vidal de la Blache: "Conception resulting from a more synthetic knowledge of the physical laws governing our earth and of the relations between the living beings which inhabit it."

    Key Notes

    • Human geography studies the inter-relationship between the physical environment and the socio-cultural environment created by human beings.
    • Geography is subjected to dualism — debates on whether it should be nomothetic (law-making) or idiographic (descriptive); regional or systematic; theoretical or historic-institutional.
    • The dichotomy between physical and human geography is not fully valid — nature and humans are inseparable and must be seen holistically.

    Naturalisation of Humans ↔ Humanisation of Nature

    ConceptMeaning
    Environmental DeterminismPrimitive society + low technology → nature dictates human life; the "naturalised human" who worshipped and feared nature.
    PossibilismWith better technology, nature offers opportunities that humans exploit — nature gets "humanised," bearing the imprint of human endeavour (health resorts, urban sprawls, ports, satellites).
    Neo-determinism / Stop-and-go determinismProposed by Griffith Taylor — a middle path (Madhyam Marg): humans can conquer nature by obeying it, like traffic lights (stop/get set/go); avoids the free run that caused the greenhouse effect, ozone depletion, and receding glaciers.
    • Naturalisation of humans: illustrated by Benda, a tribal in the Abujh Maad area of central India, practising shifting cultivation (penda) and worshipping the forest spirit Loi-Lugi — direct dependence on nature as "Mother Nature."
    • Humanisation of nature: illustrated by Kari in Trondheim, Norway — technology (heated glass-dome campus, imported tropical fruit, flights) overcomes the constraints of a harsh winter climate.

    Table 1.1 — Broad Stages and Thrust of Human Geography

    PeriodApproach
    Early Colonial periodExploration and description
    Later Colonial period (1930s–inter-war)Regional analysis / Areal differentiation
    Late 1950s–late 1960sSpatial organisation (quantitative revolution)
    1970sEmergence of humanistic, radical and behavioural schools
    1990sPost-modernism in geography
    • Welfare/Humanistic school: social well-being — housing, health, education.
    • Radical school: uses Marxian theory to explain poverty, deprivation and inequality via capitalism.
    • Behavioural school: emphasis on lived experience and perception of space by ethnicity, race, religion.

    Remember it as

    Environmental Determinism (nature rules) → Possibilism (humans exploit nature) → Neo-determinism (Griffith Taylor's traffic-light 'stop and go'). Quantitative revolution = late 1950s-60s; three new schools (humanistic/radical/behavioural) = 1970s.

    02Fields and Sub-fields of Human Geography

    Human geography's reach is so wide that it has grown a dedicated sub-field for almost every sister discipline in the social sciences.

    NCERT — Interdisciplinary Nature

    Human geography attempts to explain the relationship between all elements of human life and the space they occur over. Thus, human geography assumes a highly inter-disciplinary nature, developing close interfaces with sister disciplines in the social sciences.

    Table 1.2 — Human Geography and Sister Disciplines

    FieldSub-fieldSister Discipline
    Social GeographyBehavioural GeographyPsychology
    Geography of Social Well-beingEconomics
    Cultural/HistoricalCultural GeographyAnthropology
    Gender GeographySociology, Anthropology, Women's Studies
    Historical GeographyHistory
    Urban Geography—Urban Studies and Planning
    Political GeographyElectoral GeographyPsephology
    Military GeographyMilitary Science
    Population Geography—Demography
    Economic GeographyGeography of ResourcesResource Economics
    Geography of AgricultureAgricultural Sciences
    Geography of IndustriesIndustrial Economics
    Geography of MarketingBusiness Studies, Commerce
    Geography of TourismTourism and Travel Management
    Geography of International TradeInternational Trade

    Remember it as

    Every sub-field pairs with a named sister discipline: Electoral Geography ↔ Psephology, Population Geography ↔ Demography, Medical Geography ↔ Epidemiology — these named pairings are the most CUET-testable part of this table.

    01Patterns of Population Distribution & Density

    "Asia has many places where people are few and few places where people are very many" — true of the whole world, not just Asia.

    NCERT — Population Distribution

    Population distribution refers to the way people are spaced over the earth's surface. Broadly, 90 per cent of the world's population lives in about 10 per cent of its land area.

    Key Notes

    • The 10 most populous countries of the world contribute about 60% of the world's population — of these, 6 are in Asia.
    • Density of Population = Population ÷ Area (persons per sq km) — e.g. Region X: 1,50,000 persons ÷ 100 sq km = 1,500 persons/sq km.

    Factors Influencing Population Distribution

    CategoryFactors
    GeographicalWater availability (river valleys densely populated), Landforms (plains favoured over mountains — Ganga plains vs Himalayan zones), Climate (moderate climates preferred — Mediterranean regions), Soils (fertile loamy soils support intensive agriculture)
    EconomicMinerals (e.g. Katanga-Zambia copper belt, Africa), Urbanisation (cities pull rural migrants), Industrialisation (e.g. Kobe-Osaka region, Japan)
    Social & CulturalReligious/cultural significance attracts people; social/political unrest repels them; government incentives can redirect population

    Remember it as

    90% of world population on just 10% of land. Top 10 countries = 60% of world population, 6 of them in Asia. Density = Population ÷ Area.

    02Population Growth — Concepts & Components

    Population change is never just one number — it splits into growth, growth rate, natural growth and actual growth, each measuring something subtly different.

    NCERT — Basic Concepts

    Growth of Population: change in population of a particular area between two points in time. Natural Growth = Births − Deaths. Actual Growth = Births − Deaths + In-migration − Out-migration.

    Key Notes

    • Example: India's population 2001 (102.70 crore) → 2011 (121.02 crore) = growth of 18.15 crore in absolute numbers.
    • Positive growth: birth rate > death rate, or net in-migration. Negative growth: birth rate < death rate, or net out-migration.
    • Crude Birth Rate (CBR) = (Live births during year ÷ Estimated mid-year population) × 1,000.
    • Crude Death Rate (CDR) = (Deaths during year ÷ Estimated mid-year population) × 1,000 — affected by demographic structure, social advancement, economic development.
    • Human population increased more than 10 times in the past 500 years; in the 20th century alone it increased 4 times.

    CBR & CDR — the formulas

    Crude Birth Rate

    CBR = (B ÷ P) × 1000   [B = live births, P = mid-year population]

    Crude Death Rate

    CDR = (D ÷ P) × 1000   [D = deaths, P = mid-year population]

    Remember it as

    Natural Growth = Births − Deaths. Actual Growth = Natural Growth ± Migration. Population grew 10× in 500 years, 4× in the 20th century alone.

    03Migration — Push & Pull Factors

    Migration is a spontaneous effort to balance population against resources — and every migrant is, simultaneously, both an emigrant and an immigrant.

    NCERT — Migration

    Migrants who move INTO a new place are Immigrants; migrants who move OUT of a place are Emigrants. The place moved from is the Place of Origin (population decreases); the place moved to is the Place of Destination (population increases).

    Key Notes

    • Migration may be permanent, temporary, or seasonal; rural-rural, rural-urban, urban-urban, or urban-rural.
    • Push factors (origin becomes unattractive): unemployment, poor living conditions, political turmoil, unpleasant climate, natural disasters, epidemics, socio-economic backwardness.
    • Pull factors (destination becomes attractive): better job opportunities, better living conditions, peace/stability, security, pleasant climate.

    Remember it as

    Immigrant = moves IN. Emigrant = moves OUT. Push = origin repels (unemployment, disaster). Pull = destination attracts (jobs, security, climate).

    04Demographic Transition & Population Control

    Every society, the theory says, eventually moves from high births and high deaths to low births and low deaths — just at very different speeds.

    NCERT — Demographic Transition Theory

    Population of any region changes from high births and high deaths to low births and low deaths as society progresses from rural agrarian/illiterate to urban industrial/literate. These changes occur in stages, together known as the demographic cycle.

    Three Stages of Demographic Transition

    StageCharacteristics
    Stage I — High FluctuatingHigh fertility AND high mortality; slow growth; large families valued (agrarian); low life expectancy, illiteracy, low technology. All countries were here 200 years ago.
    Stage II — ExpandingFertility stays high initially but mortality falls (better sanitation/health) → high net addition to population.
    Stage III — Low FluctuatingBoth fertility and mortality decline considerably; population stable or slow-growing; urbanised, literate, high technical know-how, deliberate family-size control.

    Population Control Measures

    • Family planning: spacing/preventing births — key to limiting growth and improving women's health; helped by propaganda, free contraceptives, tax disincentives for large families.
    • Thomas Malthus (1798): population grows faster than food supply; further increase → population crash via famine, disease, war. Preventive checks are better than positive/physical checks.

    Remember it as

    Stage I = high births + high deaths (agrarian). Stage II = high births, falling deaths (expanding). Stage III = low births + low deaths (industrial). Malthus (1798) = population outgrows food supply.

    01Growth, Development & the Concept of Human Development

    A city's population can double without a single life getting better — growth and development are not the same thing.

    Growth vs Development

    Growth is quantitative and value-neutral — it may be positive or negative. Development means a qualitative change which is always value-positive — it cannot happen without an increment to existing conditions.

    Key Notes

    • Example: a city's population growing from 1 lakh to 2 lakh is growth. If housing, basic services and other facilities stay the same, this growth has NOT been accompanied by development.
    • For decades, a country's development was measured only by economic growth (GNP) — even when this growth did not change the lives of most people.
    • The concept of human development was introduced by Pakistani economist Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq — development that enlarges people's choices and improves their lives.
    • Prof. Amartya Sen (Nobel Laureate) saw an increase in freedom (or decrease in unfreedom) as development's main objective; his work explores social/political institutions' role in expanding freedom.
    • Since 1990, the UNDP has published the Human Development Report annually, using Dr Haq's concept.

    Four Pillars of Human Development

    PillarMeaning
    EquityEqual access to opportunities for everybody, regardless of gender, race, income or caste.
    SustainabilityContinuity in availability of opportunities — each generation must have the same opportunities as the last.
    ProductivityHuman labour productivity, built by enriching people's capabilities — people are the real wealth of nations.
    EmpowermentThe power to make choices, coming from increased freedom and capability — especially for socially/economically disadvantaged groups.
    • Very often people lack the capability and freedom to make even basic choices — due to lack of knowledge, poverty, social discrimination, or weak institutions.
    • Building capabilities in health, education and access to resources is key to enlarging people's choices.
    • Bhutan is the only country to officially proclaim Gross National Happiness (GNH) as its measure of progress — material progress is approached cautiously to protect environment and spiritual/cultural life.

    Remember it as

    Growth = quantitative, value-neutral. Development = qualitative, always value-positive. Mahbub-ul-Haq = enlarging choices. Amartya Sen = increasing freedom. 4 pillars: Equity, Sustainability, Productivity, Empowerment.

    02Human Development Index & Approaches to Human Development

    Four very different schools of thought have tried to answer the same question: what actually makes a country "developed"?

    Human Development Index (HDI)

    The HDI ranks countries based on performance in health, education and access to resources, scored between 0 and 1. Each dimension gets a weightage of 1/3. The closer the score to 1, the greater the level of human development.

    Key Notes — How HDI is Measured

    • Health → Life expectancy at birth.
    • Access to knowledge → Adult literacy rate + Gross enrolment ratio.
    • Access to resources → Purchasing power, measured in US dollars.
    • The Human Poverty Index (HPI) is related but different — it measures the shortfall in human development (non-income measure): probability of not surviving to 40, adult illiteracy, lack of access to clean water, underweight children. HPI is often more revealing than HDI alone.

    Four Approaches to Human Development

    ApproachCore Idea
    (a) Income ApproachOne of the oldest — human development is linked to income; higher income = higher level of freedom = higher development.
    (b) Welfare ApproachPeople are beneficiaries/targets, not participants; argues for higher government expenditure on education, health, social security.
    (c) Basic Needs ApproachProposed by the ILO; identifies six basic needs — health, education, food, water supply, sanitation, housing. Ignores human choice.
    (d) Capability ApproachAssociated with Prof. Amartya Sen; building capabilities in health, education and access to resources is key to increasing human development.

    Remember it as

    HDI = ⅓ health + ⅓ knowledge + ⅓ resources. 4 approaches: Income (oldest), Welfare (govt-driven), Basic Needs (ILO, 6 needs), Capability (Amartya Sen).

    03International Comparisons of Human Development

    Size of territory and per-capita income don't decide human development — smaller, even relatively poorer nations often outrank bigger, richer ones.

    NCERT — International Comparisons

    Sri Lanka and Trinidad and Tobago rank higher than India in HDI despite smaller economies. Within India, Kerala performs much better than Punjab and Gujarat in human development, despite lower per-capita income.

    Table 3.2 — Human Development Categories (Human Development Report, 2025)

    LevelHDI ScoreNo. of Countries
    Very Highabove 0.80074
    High0.700 – 0.79950
    Medium0.550 – 0.69953
    Lowbelow 0.55026

    Table 3.3 — Top Ten Ranked Countries (HDI, 2025)

    RankCountry
    1Iceland
    2Norway
    3Switzerland
    4Denmark
    5Germany / Sweden
    7Australia
    8Hong Kong (SAR, China) / Netherlands
    10Belgium

    Most Very-High HDI countries are former imperial powers, mostly located in Europe with relatively low social diversity — but several non-European countries also feature.

    Key Notes — Group Characteristics

    • Very High group (74 countries): high government investment in social sectors, higher social diversity in the Medium group, good governance.
    • Medium group (53 countries, the largest): mostly countries that emerged after WWII or the Soviet breakup (1990); adopting more people-oriented policies.
